thevenin.title: Replace a divider
thevenin.prompt: A 15 V ideal source feeds a 3 kΩ resistor above the output and a 6 kΩ resistor from output to ground. Find the Thévenin equivalent seen by an external load. Then connect an 8 kΩ load and find its voltage and current.
thevenin.hint: Remove only the external load. For resistance, replace the independent ideal voltage source by a short.

solution.step: Identify the port and remove only the load
solution.text: The output node and ground form the port. The 3 kΩ and 6 kΩ resistors belong to the source network, so both stay in the model.
With nothing connected, the two resistors form an unloaded divider.
Replace the ideal 15 V source by a short. Looking into the port, the 3 kΩ and 6 kΩ resistors now both go to ground, so they are in parallel.
The load and $R_{th}$ form a series loop driven by $V_{th}$.
The lower branch becomes 6 kΩ ∥ 8 kΩ = 3.4286 kΩ.

solution.answer: Thévenin equivalent: 10 V in series with 2 kΩ. With 8 kΩ connected: 8 V and 1 mA.

thevenin.title: A negative branch current
thevenin.prompt: Two sources share ground. The output is connected to a 5 V source through 1 kΩ and to a 1 V source through 3 kΩ. Find the equivalent, then the output with a 750 Ω load. Find both source-branch currents, positive toward the output.
thevenin.hint: Use the conductance-weighted average for the open-circuit voltage. A negative branch current means the ideal source absorbs current.

solution.text: With no load, the output node's KCL says the two branch currents sum to zero. Solving gives a conductance-weighted average of the source voltages.
Short both ideal sources; the 1 kΩ and 3 kΩ resistors are then in parallel.
Equal source and load resistances split $V_{th}$ in half.
Each branch current, positive toward the output, is (source voltage − output voltage)/resistance.
$3 - 0.333 = 2.667$ mA, which equals the load current. The negative sign means current flows into the 1 V source, which an ideal source accepts but a real supply may not.

solution.answer: $V_{th}$ = 4 V and $R_{th}$ = 750 Ω. With the load: 2 V output, +3 mA from the 5 V branch, −0.333 mA in the 1 V branch.

thevenin.title: Measure the slope with a test source
thevenin.prompt: After independent sources are deactivated, a port has a 1 kΩ resistor to ground and a parallel dependent source injecting 0.6Vₜ/(1 kΩ) upward from ground into the port. Find its resistance using a 2 V test source. Explain why you must not remove the dependent source.
thevenin.hint: The resistor draws current while the dependent source supplies part of it. The test source supplies the difference.

solution.text: Only independent sources are deactivated. The dependent source depends on the port voltage $V_t$, so it is part of the port's behaviour and must remain.
Connect $V_t$ = 2 V and define the test current $I_t$ flowing into the network.
The resistor draws $V_t/1\ \text{k}\Omega$ to ground, and the dependent source supplies $0.6V_t/1\ \text{k}\Omega$ of it. The test source supplies the rest.
The dependent source carries 60% of the resistor's current, so the port's current-voltage slope is only 40% as steep and the resistance is 1 kΩ/0.4. Removing the source would wrongly give 1 kΩ.

solution.answer: $R_{th}$ = 2.5 kΩ. The dependent source must stay because it changes the slope of the port's I–V relationship.

thevenin.title: Power or voltage accuracy?
thevenin.prompt: An ideal Thévenin model has $V_{\mathrm{th}}$ = 6 V and $R_{\mathrm{th}}$ = 200 Ω. Which resistive load receives maximum power, and how much? Compare its output voltage and model efficiency with a 1.8 kΩ load.
thevenin.hint: Maximum power occurs at $R_L$ = $R_{\mathrm{th}}$ for positive real resistances. Model efficiency is load power divided by the ideal source’s delivered power.

solution.text: For a real source resistance, load power $V_{th}^2R_L/(R_{th}+R_L)^2$ peaks when $R_L = R_{th}$ = 200 Ω.
At the matched load, half of $V_{th}$ appears across the load.
The 200 Ω source resistance carries the same current and also dissipates 45 mW, so the source delivers 90 mW.
The matched load gets more power but loses half the source voltage. The 1.8 kΩ load gets less power but keeps 90% of the voltage. Choose by goal: power transfer or voltage accuracy and efficiency.

solution.answer: Maximum power is 45 mW into 200 Ω at 3 V and 50% efficiency. With 1.8 kΩ: 5.4 V, 16.2 mW, 90% model efficiency.

small-signal.title: Two answers, two questions
small-signal.prompt: A diode is biased at 0.62 V and 1 mA. Near that point, assume an exponential model with n = 2, $V_T$ = 25.85 mV, and negligible $I_s$ compared with bias current. Find its DC ratio, differential resistance, and predicted voltage change for a +20 µA current change.
small-signal.hint: The DC ratio uses the full voltage and current. The differential resistance is nVₜ/IQ.

solution.text: This is the ratio of total voltage to total current, which describes the operating point.
With $I\approx I_se^{V/nV_T}$, the slope is $dI/dV = I/nV_T$. Its reciprocal is the differential resistance.

solution.step: Use the local model for the change

solution.text: Inverting the exponential gives $\Delta V = nV_T\ln(I_2/I_1)$.
The two agree within 1% because the current changes by only 2%. Using the DC ratio would predict 620 Ω × 20 µA = 12.4 mV, the answer to a different question.

solution.answer: $R_{DC}$ = 620 Ω, $r_d$ = 51.7 Ω, $\Delta V$ ≈ 1.03 mV.

small-signal.title: A signal across a biased diode
small-signal.prompt: A diode with n = 1 is biased at 0.5 mA at 300 K. A source drives it through 2 kΩ. For a +5 mV source perturbation, estimate the diode’s voltage and current changes using the local model.
small-signal.hint: Find $r_d$, then use the series combination 2 kΩ + $r_d$. The signal across the diode is smaller than the source signal.

solution.step: Replace the diode by $r_d$ for the signal
solution.text: Around the operating point the circuit becomes a resistive divider: 2 kΩ in series with 51.7 Ω, driven by the 5 mV perturbation.

solution.step: Find the signal across the diode
Check that the local model is valid
solution.text: $v_d/V_T = 0.126/25.85 \approx 0.005$, far below 1, so the curvature of the exponential is negligible.

solution.answer: The diode current rises by 2.44 µA (to 0.5024 mA) and its voltage by only 0.126 mV.

small-signal.title: Positive and negative are not symmetric
small-signal.prompt: For a 1 mA diode bias with n = 1 and $V_T$ = 25.85 mV, compare the linear and exponential current changes for voltage perturbations of +10 mV and −10 mV. Neglect $I_s$ relative to bias current.
small-signal.hint: The linear estimate is IQ·v/$V_T$. The exact change is IQ[exp(v/$V_T$) − 1].

solution.text: The tangent slope at the bias point is $I_Q/V_T$.
Scaling the exponential from the bias point gives $I=I_Qe^{v/V_T}$.

The tangent predicts equal and opposite changes. The exponential curves upward, so the positive step gives more current than predicted and the negative step less. Total currents are 1.472 mA and 0.679 mA; both remain positive.

solution.answer: Linear: ±0.387 mA. Exact: +0.472 mA and −0.321 mA. The asymmetry is the curvature the linear model ignores.

small-signal.title: Read a slope without a diode formula
small-signal.prompt: Near VQ = 0.5 V, a device follows I(V) = 0.001 + 0.004(V − 0.5) + 0.02(V − 0.5)², with volts and amperes used consistently. Find its bias current, DC ratio, and small-signal resistance. For a +10 mV change, compare the exact and linear current changes.
small-signal.hint: Differentiate with respect to V and evaluate at 0.5 V. The quadratic term affects a finite change even though its derivative is zero at Q.

solution.step: Find the bias current and DC ratio
solution.text: At $V$ = 0.5 V both correction terms vanish.

solution.step: Invert to get the small-signal resistance

solution.text: Substitute $V - 0.5$ = 0.01 V into the full expression.
The linear estimate is low by 2/42 = 4.76%. The quadratic term has zero slope at Q but still contributes over a finite step.

solution.answer: $I_Q$ = 1 mA, $R_{DC}$ = 500 Ω, $r_d$ = 250 Ω. For +10 mV: linear 40 µA, exact 42 µA.

power.title: A nominal quarter watt
power.prompt: An exact 9 V is applied across a nominal 330 Ω resistor with ±5% tolerance. Find nominal current and power, then worst-case power. Does a 0.25 W rating provide enough capacity even before temperature derating?
power.hint: With voltage fixed, lower resistance causes higher dissipation.

solution.text: With the voltage fixed, $P=V^2/R$ is largest at the lowest resistance, which is 5% below nominal.
0.258 W exceeds 0.25 W before any derating for ambient temperature or mounting. Even the nominal value uses 98% of the rating.

solution.answer: Nominal: 27.3 mA, 0.245 W. Worst case: 0.258 W. A 0.25 W part is not adequate; choose 0.5 W or larger.

power.title: Average is not the whole story
power.prompt: A 220 Ω resistor carries 100 mA for 2 ms every 20 ms, and no current otherwise. Find peak power, average power, RMS current, and energy per pulse. Is a 0.25 W continuous rating alone enough to approve the part?
power.hint: Duty cycle is 0.1. RMS current is peak current times the square root of duty cycle for these rectangular pulses.

solution.text: For rectangular pulses, $I_{rms}=I_{pk}\sqrt{D}$. As a check, $I_{rms}^2R$ = 0.22 W.
The average is below 0.25 W but leaves little margin. A continuous rating says nothing about 2.2 W for 2 ms, so check the pulse-energy curve, working voltage, tolerance and thermal derating.

solution.answer: 2.2 W peak, 0.22 W average, 31.6 mA RMS, 4.4 mJ per pulse. The continuous rating alone is not enough to approve the part.

power.title: A warm-up in two numbers
power.prompt: A one-node thermal model starts at 35 °C ambient. Constant dissipation is 0.4 W, Rθ = 80 °C/W, and Cθ = 3 J/°C. Find its final temperature, time constant, and temperature after one and three time constants.
power.hint: Find the final temperature rise first. Multiply the rise by 1 − exp(−t/$\tau$), then add ambient.

solution.text: At equilibrium all the heat flows through $R_\theta$.

solution.answer: Final 67 °C, τ = 240 s, 55.2 °C after one τ and 65.4 °C after three.

power.title: A regulator’s missing constraint
power.prompt: A linear regulator converts 9 V to 3.3 V at 150 mA. Ignore quiescent current. Local ambient may reach 60 °C, and the design junction-temperature target is 105 °C. Find the largest allowed effective thermal resistance. If the actual system provides 70 °C/W, find the predicted temperature and maximum current meeting the target.
power.hint: Dissipation is voltage drop times load current. Solve the thermal equation once for resistance and once for current.

solution.text: A linear regulator drops the input-output difference while carrying the load current.
Set $T_J$ = 105 °C with $P=(V_{in}-V_{out})I$.

solution.step: State the limits of the model
solution.text: This assumes constant ambient and thermal resistance and ignores quiescent current; the regulator's own electrical limits still apply.

solution.answer: Need $R_\theta$ ≤ 52.6 °C/W. At 70 °C/W the junction reaches ≈120 °C, so current must be limited to ≈113 mA.

capacitors.title: A pulse on a precharged capacitor
capacitors.prompt: A 22 µF ideal capacitor starts at 1 V. A +0.5 mA current enters its positive terminal for 44 ms. Find final voltage, final plate charge, and the increase in stored energy.
capacitors.hint: Find added charge first, then use the difference between final and initial energies.

solution.text: Subtract the energies. Using ½C(ΔV)² would give only 11 µJ because energy is not linear in voltage.

solution.answer: Final voltage 2 V, charge 44 µC, stored energy up by 33 µJ.

capacitors.title: Where did the stored energy go?
capacitors.prompt: An isolated 10 µF capacitor at 6 V is connected in parallel with a 20 µF capacitor at 0 V, with matching polarity. Find the final voltage and the decrease in capacitor energy after settling.
capacitors.hint: Total signed charge is conserved. Total capacitance after connection is 30 µF.

solution.text: The capacitors are isolated, so total charge is fixed.
In parallel the capacitances add to 30 µF.
120 µJ leaves the capacitors. It is dissipated in the connecting resistance (or radiated), however small that resistance is.

solution.answer: Final voltage 2 V; capacitor energy falls by 120 µJ (from 180 to 60 µJ).

capacitors.title: Unequal capacitances, unequal voltages
capacitors.prompt: Two initially uncharged ideal capacitors, 4.7 µF and 10 µF, are connected in series across 12 V. Their isolated middle node has zero net charge. Find equivalent capacitance and each final voltage.
capacitors.hint: Series charge magnitudes are equal; voltage is charge divided by capacitance.

solution.text: The isolated middle node starts at zero net charge, so both capacitors carry the same charge magnitude.
8.163 + 3.837 = 12 V. The smaller capacitor takes the larger voltage.

solution.answer: $C_{eq}$ = 3.20 µF. The 4.7 µF part has 8.16 V, the 10 µF part 3.84 V.

rc-circuits.title: Three facts from one time constant
rc-circuits.prompt: A 47 kΩ resistor charges 100 nF from 0 V toward 3.3 V. Find the time constant, voltage at one time constant, and time to reach within 1% of the final voltage.
rc-circuits.hint: The remaining error fraction is exp(−t/$\tau$).

solution.text: The fraction still to go is $e^{-t/\tau}$. Set it to 1%.

solution.answer: τ = 4.7 ms, 2.09 V at one τ, 21.6 ms to settle within 1%.

rc-circuits.title: The final voltage is not the supply
rc-circuits.prompt: A 10 V supply feeds a node through 20 kΩ. The node has 30 kΩ to ground and a 1 µF capacitor to ground. The capacitor initially holds 2 V. Find the final voltage, time constant, and voltage after one time constant.
rc-circuits.hint: Find the Thévenin equivalent seen by the capacitor.

solution.step: Reduce the network the capacitor sees
solution.text: Remove the capacitor and find the Thévenin equivalent at its terminals.
The capacitor moves from its initial value toward $V_{th}$.

solution.answer: Final voltage 6 V, τ = 12 ms, 4.53 V after one τ.

rc-circuits.title: Reach a threshold in time
rc-circuits.prompt: An ideal 5 V step charges a capacitor through 10 kΩ from zero. What is the largest C that reaches at least 3 V by 5 ms? Does 470 nF meet the nominal requirement? Ignore tolerance.
rc-circuits.hint: Set the threshold crossing equal to the latest permitted time.

solution.step: Set the threshold at the deadline

solution.text: τ = 4.7 ms, so the crossing time is $-4.7\ \text{ms}\cdot\ln0.4$ = 4.31 ms, before 5 ms.

solution.answer: $C_{max}$ ≈ 546 nF. 470 nF reaches 3 V at 4.31 ms, so it meets the nominal requirement.

differentiators.title: Check the band before differentiating
differentiators.prompt: A passive high-pass RC circuit has $\tau$ = 100 µs. Its input is a 2 V peak sine at 50 Hz. Find approximate and exact output amplitudes, exact phase, and relative complex-response error.
differentiators.hint: Compute x = 2πfτ; use H = jx/(1 + jx).

solution.text: For $x\ll1$, $H\approx jx$, so the amplitude is the input times $x$.

The exact response is $jx/(1+jx)$ and the approximation is $jx$. Their relative difference has magnitude $|jx/(1+jx)-jx|/|jx/(1+jx)| = x$ = 3.14%. Amplitude alone differs by only 0.05%, because most of the error is in phase.

solution.answer: Approximate 62.83 mV, exact 62.80 mV at 88.2°; complex-response error ≈ 3.1%.

differentiators.title: The second edge remembers the first
differentiators.prompt: A high-pass RC network has $\tau$ = 200 µs and starts uncharged. Its input steps from 0 V to 4 V, stays there for 1 ms, then returns to zero. Find output after 600 µs and immediately after the falling edge.
differentiators.hint: Superpose a +4 V step response and a delayed −4 V step response.

solution.text: The input is +4 V at $t=0$ plus −4 V at $t$ = 1 ms. A high-pass network's step response is $Ve^{-t/\tau}$.
Only the first step has occurred.

solution.step: Output just after the falling edge
solution.text: The first step has decayed for 1 ms; the second step contributes its full −4 V.
The capacitor voltage cannot change instantly, so the full −4 V edge appears at the output. Starting from 0.027 V gives −3.973 V.

solution.answer: 0.199 V at 600 µs; −3.97 V immediately after the falling edge.

differentiators.title: A derivative after startup
differentiators.prompt: A ramp rises at 0.5 V/ms from zero. A high-pass circuit has R = 10 kΩ and C = 20 nF, with zero initial state. Find the eventual ramp-response level and output after one time constant.
differentiators.hint: The exact response during the continuing ramp is sτ(1 − exp(−t/$\tau$)).

solution.text: Starting from zero state, a high-pass network driven by a ramp gives the derivative plus a startup transient.

solution.answer: Eventual level 0.1 V; after one τ (200 µs) the output is 63.2 mV.

integrators.title: Quantify the approximation
integrators.prompt: An unloaded low-pass RC network has $\tau$ = 1 ms. A 1 V peak sine at 20 kHz drives it. Find the integral approximation’s output amplitude, exact amplitude, and relative complex-response error.
integrators.hint: Use x = 2πfτ. The exact gain is 1/√(1 + x²), while the approximation is 1/x.

solution.text: For $x\gg1$, $H\approx1/(jx)$.
The relative difference between $1/(1+jx)$ and $1/(jx)$ has magnitude $1/x$. Amplitude agrees to 0.003%, but the phase is 0.46° from −90°.

solution.answer: Approximate 7.958 mV, exact 7.957 mV; complex-response error ≈ 0.80%.

integrators.title: Find the ripple amplitude
integrators.prompt: A ±2 V square wave with period 200 µs drives an RC low-pass with $\tau$ = 2 ms. Estimate the steady triangular output amplitude and compare it with the exact peak magnitude.
integrators.hint: Approximate slope is ±A/$\tau$. Each half-cycle lasts 100 µs.

solution.text: Because $\tau$ is 20 times the half-period, the output barely moves, so the resistor sees nearly the full ±2 V.
The triangle is symmetric about zero, so the peak is half the swing: 50 mV.
In steady state each exponential segment swings between $\pm V_p$.

solution.answer: Triangle of about ±50 mV; exact peak 49.99 mV.

integrators.title: Account for initial voltage
integrators.prompt: An ideal inverting integrator has R = 100 kΩ and C = 10 nF. Output starts at +1 V. A +20 mV input is applied. Find output after 50 ms and time to reach an assumed −4 V output limit.
integrators.hint: The slope is −Vin/(RC); retain the initial +1 V.

solution.text: For an inverting integrator, $dv_o/dt = -v_{in}/RC$.
The output must change by −5 V from its starting point.

solution.answer: 0 V after 50 ms; the output reaches the −4 V limit at 250 ms.

real-capacitors.title: Where the capacitor stops looking capacitive
real-capacitors.prompt: A series model has C = 100 nF, ESL = 5 nH, and ESR = 0.05 Ω. Find resonance frequency, impedance at resonance, and whether the model is capacitive or inductive at 100 MHz.

solution.text: The series model's reactances cancel when $\omega L = 1/\omega C$.
The reactances cancel, leaving only the ESR: 0.05 Ω.

solution.answer: Resonance at 7.12 MHz with |Z| = 0.05 Ω. At 100 MHz the part is inductive, about 3.13 Ω.

real-capacitors.title: Use effective capacitance
real-capacitors.prompt: A nominal 22 µF part may be 20% low and, under a stated multiplicative bias model, retain only 50% of that value at operating voltage. An extra 50 mA load lasts 100 µs. Find capacitive droop, then the ESR drop for 0.1 Ω. Neglect ESL and upstream current response.
real-capacitors.hint: Find the effective capacitance before applying ΔV = IΔt/C.

solution.text: The ESR drop appears as soon as the current flows.

solution.step: Total at the end of the pulse

solution.answer: Effective 8.8 µF gives 0.568 V of droop, plus 5 mV from ESR: about 0.573 V total.

real-capacitors.title: A small current matters during hold
real-capacitors.prompt: A 47 nF hold capacitor may droop by at most 5 mV in 20 ms. Assuming approximately constant unwanted discharge current, find its maximum total. If amplifier input current uses 5 nA and switch leakage uses 4 nA, what remains for capacitor and board leakage?
real-capacitors.hint: Use I = CΔV/Δt and add all current contributions in the unfavorable direction.

solution.step: Convert the droop limit to current

solution.text: Assume every leakage acts in the same direction.
The capacitor dielectric and board surface together must stay below 2.75 nA, including over temperature and humidity.

solution.answer: Total budget 11.75 nA; 2.75 nA remains for capacitor and board leakage.

inductors.title: Current takes time
inductors.prompt: A 3.3 V source drives a 22 mH ideal inductor through 33 Ω. Initial current is zero. Find final current, time constant, current after one time constant, and final stored energy.
inductors.hint: Use $\tau$ = L/R and the RL exponential.

solution.text: At DC the ideal inductor is a short.

solution.answer: 100 mA final, τ = 0.667 ms, 63.2 mA at one τ, 110 µJ stored.

inductors.title: Energy and release time
inductors.prompt: An isolated ideal 47 mH inductor starts at 80 mA. A one-way clamp applies a constant 24 V opposing the current until it reaches zero. Find stopping time, initial energy, and initial clamp power.
inductors.hint: Use di/dt = −Vclamp/L. The clamp absorbs the stored energy in this model.

solution.text: Power falls linearly to zero, so the absorbed energy is ½ × 1.92 W × 156.7 µs = 150.4 µJ, all of the stored energy.

solution.answer: Stops in 157 µs; 150 µJ stored; clamp power starts at 1.92 W.

inductors.title: Reactive voltage is not heating
inductors.prompt: A 2 mH inductor has 3 Ω winding resistance. It carries 20 mA RMS at 10 kHz. Find ideal inductive voltage magnitude and winding copper loss. Assume no core or frequency-dependent resistance losses.
inductors.hint: Use XL = 2πfL for the inductive part, and I²R for the winding loss.

solution.text: Only the resistance dissipates power.
$V_LI$ = 50 mVA is reactive power exchanged with the magnetic field, not heat. Including the 3 Ω, the terminal voltage is $0.02\sqrt{125.7^2+3^2}$ = 2.514 V.

solution.answer: Inductive voltage 2.51 V RMS; copper loss 1.2 mW.

transformers.title: Keep the power balanced
transformers.prompt: An ideal transformer has 200 primary turns and 50 secondary turns. The primary winding is held at 24 V RMS and the secondary drives 12 Ω. Find secondary voltage and current, primary load current, reflected resistance, and load power.
transformers.hint: Turns ratio a = 4; voltage divides by a, current transforms oppositely.

solution.text: Current transforms opposite to voltage.

solution.answer: 6 V and 0.5 A on the secondary, 0.125 A in the primary, 192 Ω reflected, 3 W.

transformers.title: Lower frequency, higher flux
transformers.prompt: A winding has 80 turns on an illustrative 40 mm² core area. It receives a 10 V RMS sine. Using V ≈ 4.44fNABpeak, find Bpeak at 20 kHz and 5 kHz. What minimum frequency keeps Bpeak at or below an illustrative 0.1 T target?
transformers.hint: Convert mm² to m². Flux is inversely proportional to frequency at fixed winding voltage.

solution.text: Flux is inversely proportional to frequency, so a quarter of the frequency gives four times the flux: 0.141 T.

solution.answer: 0.035 T at 20 kHz, 0.141 T at 5 kHz; frequency must be at least 7.04 kHz.

transformers.title: The source is not ideal
transformers.prompt: A 16 V RMS Thévenin source with 12 Ω series resistance drives the primary of an ideal transformer with a = Np/Ns = 4. The secondary load is 8 Ω. Find loaded secondary voltage, once by reflecting the load and once by reflecting the source.
transformers.hint: The primary sees a²RL. On the secondary, divide source voltage by a and resistance by a².

solution.step: Method 1: reflect the load to the primary
Method 2: reflect the source to the secondary
solution.text: Divide the voltage by $a$ and the resistance by $a^2$.

solution.answer: Both methods give 3.66 V RMS. The drop below 4 V comes from source resistance, not from the 4:1 ratio.

semiconductors.title: Minority does not mean irrelevant
semiconductors.prompt: At 300 K take intrinsic density as 10¹⁰ cm⁻³ and donors as 5 × 10¹⁵ cm⁻³. Estimate equilibrium electron and hole concentrations in neutral n-type silicon. Is the bulk negatively charged?
semiconductors.hint: Use the equilibrium mass-action relation, then charge neutrality.

solution.text: The donors are fully ionized at 300 K and far outnumber intrinsic carriers, so electrons ≈ donors.
In equilibrium $np=n_i^2$.
Positive charges are ionized donors plus holes; negative charges are electrons. With $n\approx N_D$ they balance, and the $2\times10^4$ holes are negligible.

solution.answer: $n$ ≈ 5 × 10¹⁵ cm⁻³, $p$ ≈ 2 × 10⁴ cm⁻³. The bulk is neutral: 'n-type' names the majority carrier, not a net charge.

semiconductors.title: Which side is wider?
semiconductors.prompt: An abrupt junction has $N_a$ = 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ and $N_D$ = 4 × 10¹⁶ cm⁻³. Its total depleted width is 0.60 µm. Find the width on each side.
semiconductors.hint: Equal total ionic charges need not occupy equal distances.

solution.text: The exposed acceptor charge on the p side must equal the exposed donor charge on the n side.

solution.answer: $x_n$ = 0.12 µm, $x_p$ = 0.48 µm. The lightly doped side holds most of the depletion region.

semiconductors.title: Reverse bias changes the capacitor
semiconductors.prompt: A junction has Vbi = 0.75 V and zero-bias capacitance 8 pF. In the abrupt depletion model, what is its capacitance at 3 V reverse bias? How does width change?
semiconductors.hint: Width scales as the square root of the total depletion potential; capacitance scales inversely.

solution.text: In the abrupt model $W\propto\sqrt{V_{bi}+V_R}$.
Junction capacitance is a parallel-plate capacitance $\varepsilon A/W$, so it scales as $1/W$.
This ignores breakdown and the diffusion charge that appears under forward bias.

solution.answer: Width grows by 2.24×; capacitance falls to 3.58 pF.

semiconductors.title: An internal voltage is not a battery
semiconductors.prompt: A student measures the built-in potential from a depletion calculation and proposes extracting power continuously from an unconnected PN junction. Explain the error.
semiconductors.hint: Distinguish an internal electrostatic potential from terminal electromotive force.

solution.text: In an unconnected junction at equilibrium, drift and diffusion currents cancel for both carriers. No net current flows, so no power is delivered.
Connecting wires adds metal–semiconductor contacts. Their contact potentials exactly cancel the built-in potential around the loop, so a voltmeter reads zero.
Sustained power needs a non-equilibrium energy input: light (a solar cell), heat flow (a thermoelectric device) or applied bias.

solution.answer: The built-in potential is an internal equilibrium potential, cancelled around any closed loop by contact potentials. Without an external energy source no current flows.

diodes.title: How much more voltage?
diodes.prompt: For a diode with ideality factor 1.5 and thermal voltage 25.85 mV, find the voltage change needed to move from 0.2 mA to 2 mA. Assume both currents greatly exceed saturation current.
diodes.hint: Subtract the logarithmic voltage expressions; saturation current cancels.

solution.step: Write the voltage at each current
solution.text: With $I\gg I_s$, $V=nV_T\ln(I/I_s)$.
The saturation current cancels.

solution.answer: About 89 mV per decade of current, ignoring series resistance and self-heating.

diodes.title: Three different resistances
diodes.prompt: At a 0.65 V, 1 mA operating point with n = 1 and $V_T$ = 25.85 mV, find DC ratio resistance and differential resistance. If a 1 kΩ series resistor is fed by a 10 mV small input variation, estimate the diode-voltage variation.
diodes.hint: Use the differential resistance in the incremental divider, not the DC ratio.

solution.text: For the variation, the diode acts as $r_d$ in a divider with the 1 kΩ resistor.
0.252 mV ≪ $V_T$, so the linear model holds.

solution.answer: $R_{DC}$ = 650 Ω, $r_d$ = 25.9 Ω, diode variation ≈ 0.25 mV.

diodes.title: LED corners
diodes.prompt: A supply varies from 4.5 to 5.5 V and an LED forward drop spans 1.8 to 2.2 V. Choose a resistor no smaller than required to keep current at or below 10 mA. With a 390 Ω choice, estimate current at both corners, ignoring resistor tolerance.
diodes.hint: Maximum supply and minimum forward drop give the largest current.

solution.text: Current is largest with the highest supply and lowest LED drop.

solution.step: Current with 390 Ω at both corners

solution.answer: Need $R$ ≥ 370 Ω. With 390 Ω the current ranges 5.9–9.5 mA.

diodes.title: Time is not charge
diodes.prompt: A reverse-recovery current is approximated by a triangle with 0.3 A peak and total duration 80 ns. Estimate recovery charge. Can duration alone give switching energy?
diodes.hint: Area gives charge; energy needs voltage as well.

solution.step: Charge is the area under current
solution.text: For a triangle, area = ½ × base × height.
Energy is $\int v\,i\,dt$. Duration and peak current describe only the current waveform; the voltage across the diode during recovery also matters.
A recovery time or charge alone cannot give energy. You need the overlapping voltage waveform, which depends on the circuit.

solution.answer: $Q_{rr}$ ≈ 12 nC. No: energy also needs the voltage during recovery.

rectifiers.title: Choose a reservoir
rectifiers.prompt: A full-wave 50 Hz source feeds a 30 mA approximately constant load. What capacitance gives at most 0.5 V p-p ripple in the small-ripple estimate? What ripple would 680 µF predict?
rectifiers.hint: The recharge frequency is twice the AC frequency.

solution.text: A full-wave rectifier recharges twice per cycle: 100 Hz.
Between peaks the capacitor supplies the load for about one recharge period, so $\Delta V\approx I/(f_rC)$.

solution.answer: About 600 µF for 0.5 V; 680 µF gives ≈ 0.44 V p-p.

rectifiers.title: Will the regulator stay above dropout?
rectifiers.prompt: Minimum AC voltage is 6 V RMS. Use a bridge with two 0.8 V drops and a 40 mA load at 50 Hz, with 470 µF reservoir. Ignoring source sag, estimate peak and trough and compare the trough with a 5 V regulator needing 0.5 V dropout.
rectifiers.hint: Convert RMS to peak before subtracting diode drops and estimated ripple.

solution.text: Convert RMS to peak and subtract two bridge drops.
The regulator needs 5 + 0.5 = 5.5 V. Margin is 0.53 V before source sag and component tolerances.

solution.answer: Peak 6.89 V, trough 6.03 V: about 0.53 V above the 5.5 V needed.

rectifiers.title: A charged half-wave supply
rectifiers.prompt: An ideal half-wave rectifier charges a reservoir from a sine with 10 V peak. With negligible discharge, what reverse voltage appears across the diode at the negative source peak?
rectifiers.hint: The cathode stays near the positive peak while the anode goes negative.

solution.text: The reservoir charges to the positive peak and barely discharges, so the cathode stays at +10 V.

solution.step: Anode voltage at the negative peak
solution.text: The anode follows the source to −10 V.

solution.answer: The diode sees 20 V reverse, twice the source peak.

rectifiers.title: Where do the pulses go?
rectifiers.prompt: A reservoir feeds 25 mA DC. Recharge happens every 10 ms and is approximated by triangular source-current pulses lasting 2 ms. Find the required pulse peak and average capacitor current in settled operation.
rectifiers.hint: One pulse must supply the entire load charge for 10 ms.

solution.step: Charge drawn by the load per cycle

solution.text: In steady state each pulse must replace all of it. A triangle has area ½ × peak × width.
The capacitor's charge returns to the same value each cycle, so its average current is zero. Its RMS current is not zero and heats the ESR.

solution.answer: Pulse peak 250 mA (10× the load); average capacitor current 0.

regulators.title: Find the allowed resistor range
regulators.prompt: A 5.1 V zener regulator has input 9–15 V and load 0–10 mA. Require at least 2 mA zener current and no more than 40 mA. Find the allowable nominal resistor interval.
regulators.hint: Use minimum input/maximum load for the upper R bound, and maximum input/no load for the lower bound.

solution.text: At minimum input and full load, R must still pass the 10 mA load plus 2 mA zener minimum.
At maximum input with no load, all the current goes into the zener, which must stay ≤ 40 mA.

solution.step: Check a value inside the range
solution.text: With 300 Ω: worst-case minimum zener current is 3.9/300 − 10 mA = 3 mA; maximum is 9.9/300 = 33 mA.

solution.answer: 247.5 Ω ≤ R ≤ 325 Ω; 300 Ω works with margin, before tolerance.

regulators.title: Current rating is not enough
regulators.prompt: A linear regulator supplies 5 V at 250 mA from 12 V. Use 50 °C/W junction-to-ambient resistance and 40 °C ambient; ignore quiescent current. Estimate junction temperature. If a design target is 110 °C, what maximum current follows from this thermal model?
regulators.hint: Calculate allowable heat before dividing by the voltage drop.

solution.answer: $T_J$ ≈ 128 °C; the 110 °C target allows only 200 mA.

regulators.title: Headroom comes first
regulators.prompt: A 5 V regulator needs 0.4 V dropout and has 40 dB PSRR at the ripple frequency under regulated conditions. Input is 6 V mean with 0.4 V p-p ripple. Estimate output ripple. Then lower the input mean to 5.3 V: can the same PSRR be assumed?
regulators.hint: Compare the input trough with 5.4 V.

solution.text: The trough is the mean minus half the ripple. The regulator needs 5.4 V.
40 dB is a factor of 100.
Part of each cycle is in dropout, where the output follows the input and the PSRR figure no longer applies.

solution.answer: 4 mV p-p at 6 V mean. At 5.3 V the regulator drops out at each trough, so the PSRR cannot be assumed.

regulators.title: A zener is not perfectly stiff
regulators.prompt: A zener has 8 Ω dynamic resistance at its operating point and is fed through 220 Ω. With a high-impedance load, estimate output change for a 0.5 V small input change and for a 2 mA load-current increase at fixed input.
regulators.hint: Use an incremental divider for line change and a parallel resistance for load change.

solution.text: Replace the zener by its 8 Ω dynamic resistance; the 220 Ω feed and 8 Ω form a divider.
Looking back from the output with the input fixed: 220 Ω ∥ 8 Ω.

solution.answer: +17.5 mV for the line step; −15.4 mV for the load step.

diode-applications.title: Trace both polarities
diode-applications.prompt: A high-impedance input is clamped to ground and 3.3 V rails through fixed 0.3 V diodes, with 4.7 kΩ series resistance. Find output and resistor current at input +10 V and −10 V.
diode-applications.hint: Define resistor current positive from source toward output.

solution.text: The input pulls the output up until the upper diode turns on, so the output clamps at 3.3 + 0.3 = 3.6 V.
The output stops at one diode drop below ground: −0.3 V.
At +10 V the current flows into the 3.3 V rail. At −10 V it flows out of ground through the lower diode back toward the source.

solution.answer: +10 V: 3.6 V, 1.36 mA into the rail. −10 V: −0.3 V, −2.06 mA drawn from ground.

diode-applications.title: Budget leakage
diode-applications.prompt: A peak detector must droop by no more than 5 mV over 20 ms. Total worst-case leakage is 50 nA. What ideal capacitance is needed?
diode-applications.hint: Use charge balance over the hold interval.

solution.text: A larger C droops less but needs more charge to acquire each peak, which slows the detector.

solution.answer: At least 200 nF.

diode-applications.title: Shift, do not amplify
diode-applications.prompt: A ±3 V square wave passes through a series capacitor to an output with a large resistor to ground. A diode from ground anode to output cathode fixes the negative output near −0.6 V. Neglect droop after settling. Find the positive output.
diode-applications.hint: The input changes by 6 V on the rising edge; capacitor voltage cannot jump.

solution.text: On negative half-cycles the diode conducts and holds the output at −0.6 V.
The input jumps from −3 V to +3 V, a 6 V step. The capacitor voltage cannot change instantly, so the output also rises 6 V.

solution.answer: The output swings from −0.6 V to +5.4 V: still 6 V p-p, shifted up.

diode-applications.title: The missing sink
diode-applications.prompt: An upper protection diode injects 2 mA into an otherwise unloaded 3.3 V rail with 10 µF capacitance. Its regulator cannot sink current. Ignoring other paths, estimate the rail rise in 1 ms.
diode-applications.hint: Treat the rail capacitor as the destination of injected charge.

solution.text: The regulator cannot sink current and nothing else draws from the rail, so the injected current charges the rail capacitor.

solution.answer: The rail rises about 0.2 V per ms, so the clamp level rises with it.

diode-protection.title: A diode or a higher clamp?
diode-protection.prompt: A winding has L = 100 mH, R = 120 Ω and initial current 100 mA. Compare decay-to-zero times for 0.7 V and 24 V clamps across the winding. Find nominal switch voltage in a 12 V low-side circuit.
diode-protection.hint: Use the exponential winding model, then add supply and clamp voltages.

solution.text: While the clamp conducts, the winding sees $-V_C$. Current decays exponentially toward $-V_C/R$ and the clamp stops conducting at zero.
The clamp is across the winding, so the switch sees supply plus clamp: 12.7 V or 36 V.

solution.answer: Diode: 2.42 ms, switch at 12.7 V. 24 V clamp: 0.34 ms, switch at 36 V.

diode-protection.title: Solve for clamp voltage
diode-protection.prompt: For the same 100 mH, 120 Ω, 100 mA winding, choose a constant opposing clamp voltage that brings current to zero in 0.5 ms. What switch voltage follows with a 12 V supply?
diode-protection.hint: Exponentiate the time-to-zero expression and rearrange.

solution.answer: $V_C$ ≈ 14.6 V; switch sees about 26.6 V.

diode-protection.title: Count the energy
diode-protection.prompt: A clamp across a winding absorbs 0.378 mJ per release, with 100 releases/s. Its initial voltage/current are 24 V and 100 mA. Find average clamp power and initial pulse power. Is average power sufficient for rating?
diode-protection.hint: Differentiate energy per event from instantaneous power.

solution.text: Each event is a 2.4 W pulse. The clamp must handle the pulse energy, peak current and transient heating, not just 38 mW on average.

solution.answer: 37.8 mW average, 2.4 W initial pulse. Average power alone is not sufficient.

diode-protection.title: Move the clamp, change the energy
diode-protection.prompt: A 12 V source feeds an ideal 100 mH inductor initially carrying 100 mA. A 36 V clamp is placed across the low-side switch to ground. Ignore winding resistance. Find decay time, initial stored energy, supply energy delivered during decay and clamp energy.
diode-protection.hint: The inductor sees 12 − 36 = −24 V. Current declines linearly; integrate the triangular current waveform.

solution.text: With the switch off, the inductor connects from 12 V to the 36 V clamp node.
The current falls linearly, a triangle.
The same charge flows out of the supply and through the clamp.

solution.answer: Decay in 0.417 ms; 0.5 mJ stored, 0.25 mJ from the supply, 0.75 mJ in the clamp.

protection-circuits.title: Schottky or MOSFET on USB power?
protection-circuits.prompt: A device draws 1.5 A from a nominal 5 V USB supply that may fall to 4.75 V. Its 3.3 V regulator needs at least 4.5 V at its input. Compare a series Schottky diode dropping 0.4 V with a P-channel MOSFET of 35 mΩ on-resistance. Find the regulator input voltage and protection dissipation for each, at both 5 V and 4.75 V.
protection-circuits.hint: Series diode: subtract $V_F$ and multiply $V_F$ by I. MOSFET: subtract I·R and dissipate I²R.

solution.text: 5 V → 4.60 V; 4.75 V → 4.35 V, which is below the 4.5 V the regulator needs.
5 V → 4.95 V; 4.75 V → 4.70 V, which meets the requirement.

solution.answer: Schottky: 4.60/4.35 V (fails at low supply), 0.60 W. MOSFET: 4.95/4.70 V, 79 mW. Use the MOSFET.

protection-circuits.title: How hot does the thermistor get?
protection-circuits.prompt: A 24 V supply is switched onto an empty 2200 µF capacitor through a cold NTC thermistor of 2 Ω (treat it as a fixed resistance during charging). Find the initial current, the time constant, the energy dissipated in the thermistor, and the time to reach 95% of the final voltage.
protection-circuits.hint: Initial current is V/R. The resistor energy during a full charge does not depend on R.

solution.text: Integrating $i^2R$ over a full charge gives ½CV², independent of R.

solution.answer: 12 A initial, τ = 4.4 ms, 0.634 J in the thermistor, 95% after 13.2 ms.

protection-circuits.title: A cable that doubles the voltage
protection-circuits.prompt: A 12 V supply is hot-plugged into a board with 10 µF of ceramic input capacitance. The cable and board together contribute 1.5 µH and 30 mΩ. Estimate the characteristic impedance, peak inrush current, ringing frequency, damping ratio and peak voltage. What series resistance would give critical damping?
protection-circuits.hint: $Z_0$ = √(L/C), ζ = R/(2Z₀), and the peak of a lightly damped step is V[1 + exp(−πζ/√(1 − ζ²))].

solution.text: A lightly damped LC driven by a step peaks near $V/Z_0$.
$\zeta$ = 1 needs $R=2Z_0$ = 0.77 Ω, which wastes too much power at full current. A TVS or a damping electrolytic is more practical.

solution.answer: $Z_0$ = 0.39 Ω, ~31 A peak, 41 kHz ringing, ζ = 0.039, peak ≈ 22.6 V. Critical damping needs 0.77 Ω.

protection-circuits.title: Where does the fault current go?
protection-circuits.prompt: A 3.3 V ADC input is protected by a 4.7 kΩ series resistor and Schottky steering diodes (0.3 V) to the 3.3 V rail and ground. The cable may be shorted to ±48 V. Find the current injected into the rail for +48 V, the resistor dissipation, and the current for −48 V. In sleep the board draws 2 mA from a regulator that cannot sink current: what happens? What resistance limits injection to 1 mA?
protection-circuits.hint: With the upper diode on, the pin sits at 3.6 V. Compare the injected current with what the rail’s loads consume.

solution.text: The upper diode clamps the pin at 3.3 + 0.3 = 3.6 V.
The lower diode clamps the pin at −0.3 V.
9.45 mA is injected but only 2 mA is consumed. The regulator cannot sink the extra 7.45 mA, so the rail rises until something else conducts, possibly back-powering other chips.

solution.answer: 9.45 mA into the rail, 0.42 W in the resistor, 10.1 mA at −48 V. In sleep the rail rises. Use ≥ 44 kΩ for 1 mA.

protection-circuits.title: Size the on-time for one watt
protection-circuits.prompt: A discontinuous-mode boost circuit runs from 5 V with a 47 µH inductor at 20 kHz into a 15 V output through a 0.5 V diode. What peak current and on-time deliver 1 W to the output? Confirm the inductor current returns to zero before the next cycle.
protection-circuits.hint: Output energy per cycle is $V_{\mathrm{out}}$·$I_{\mathrm{pk}}$·$t_{\mathrm{off}}$/2 with $t_{\mathrm{off}}$ = L $I_{\mathrm{pk}}$/($V_{\mathrm{out}}$ + $V_F$ − $V_{\mathrm{in}}$). Combine and solve for $I_{\mathrm{pk}}$.

solution.step: Off-time in terms of peak current
solution.text: During release the inductor sees $V_{out}+V_F-V_{in}$ = 10.5 V.
Each cycle delivers a triangle of current to the output.

solution.answer: $I_{pk}$ ≈ 1.22 A, $t_{on}$ ≈ 11.5 µs. Current returns to zero after 17 µs, well inside the 50 µs period.

phasors.title: Both forms, carefully
phasors.prompt: Convert (a) −2 + 2j to polar form, (b) 5∠−150° to rectangular form, and (c) 1/(4 − 3j) to both forms.
phasors.hint: Sketch each arrow first so you know its quadrant. For (c), multiply by the conjugate.

solution.text: −2 + 2j points up and to the left: second quadrant.
$\arctan(2/{-2})$ returns −45°, which is in the wrong quadrant. Add 180°.
Magnitude $\sqrt{0.16^2+0.12^2}$ = 0.2, angle $\arctan(0.12/0.16)$ = 36.87°. In polar form directly: $1/(5\angle{-36.87^\circ}) = 0.2\angle36.87^\circ$.

phasors.title: Add two sinusoids
phasors.prompt: Express 4 cos(ωt + 30°) + 3 cos(ωt − 60°) as a single cosine. Why is the amplitude 5 rather than 7?

solution.step: Write each as a phasor in rectangular form

solution.text: The phasors are 30° − (−60°) = 90° apart, so they add like the sides of a right triangle: $\sqrt{4^2+3^2}$ = 5. Their peaks occur a quarter period apart and never coincide, so 7 is never reached.

solution.answer: 5 cos(ωt − 6.87°).

phasors.title: The missing volts
phasors.prompt: A resistor and capacitor are in series across a 10 V RMS sine source. A meter across the resistor reads 6 V RMS. What does a meter across the capacitor read? Explain why it is not 4 V.
phasors.hint: The resistor voltage is in phase with the current; the capacitor voltage lags it by 90°.

solution.text: Current is common to both parts. The resistor voltage is in phase with it; the capacitor voltage lags it by 90°.
The two perpendicular phasors add to the source phasor, so their magnitudes form a right triangle.
KVL holds instant by instant and for phasors, but not for RMS magnitudes of signals that peak at different times.

solution.answer: The capacitor meter reads 8 V RMS.

phasors.title: From an oscilloscope to a phasor
phasors.prompt: Two 2.5 kHz sinusoids are displayed together. Signal B crosses zero going upward 40 µs after signal A does. What is B’s phase relative to A, in degrees? Does B lead or lag?
phasors.hint: The period is 400 µs; convert the delay to a fraction of a cycle.

solution.text: B reaches the same point of its waveform later than A, so B lags.

solution.answer: B lags A by 36°: B = |B|∠−36° with A as reference.

phasors.title: An RL circuit in one line
phasors.prompt: A 5 V peak sinusoid at $\omega$ = 10⁴ rad/s drives R = 100 Ω in series with L = 10 mH. Using phasors, find the steady-state current i(t). Then verify that it satisfies L di/dt + Ri = 5 cos ωt at t = 0.
phasors.hint: Replace d/dt by jω: (R + jωL)I = V.

solution.text: Replace $d/dt$ by $j\omega$: $(R+j\omega L)\mathbf I=\mathbf V$.

solution.answer: i(t) = 35.4 cos(ωt − 45°) mA; it satisfies the circuit equation at t = 0.

impedance.title: Where do they meet?
impedance.prompt: At what frequency does a 22 nF capacitor have 1 kΩ of reactance? At what frequency does a 4.7 mH inductor? At what frequency are their reactances equal, and what is that common value?
impedance.hint: $X_C$ = 1/(2πfC) and $X_L$ = 2πfL. Setting them equal gives f = 1/(2π√LC).

solution.text: Substitute $f_0$ into either reactance.

solution.answer: Capacitor: 7.23 kHz; inductor: 33.9 kHz; equal at 15.6 kHz, where both are 462 Ω.

impedance.title: Find everything, then check Kirchhoff
impedance.prompt: A 12 V RMS, 400 Hz source drives 33 Ω in series with 15 mH. Find Z, the current, and the resistor and inductor voltages. Show that the voltages add to 12 V as phasors but not as magnitudes.
impedance.hint: $X_L$ = 2πfL. The current lags the source by ∠Z.

solution.step: Add as phasors and as magnitudes
solution.text: $V_L$ leads $V_R$ by 90°.

solution.answer: $Z$ = 50.1∠48.8° Ω, $I$ = 0.240 A, $V_R$ = 7.90 V, $V_L$ = 9.03 V. The phasor sum is 12 V; the magnitude sum (16.9 V) is not.

impedance.title: Add admittances
impedance.prompt: Find the impedance of 4.7 kΩ in parallel with 33 nF at 1 kHz, in both forms. Is the result closer to the resistor or the capacitor alone?

solution.text: In parallel, admittances add.
Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate; $|Y|^2=8.826\times10^{-8}$.
$X_C$ = 4.82 kΩ is nearly equal to R, so neither dominates: the angle is near −45° and |Z| is near $R/\sqrt2$.

solution.answer: 2411 − 2349j Ω = 3366 Ω∠−44.3°, roughly halfway between resistive and capacitive.

impedance.title: Series to parallel
impedance.prompt: A component measures Z = 30 + 40j Ω at 1 kHz. Find an equivalent parallel resistance and inductance at that frequency. Why does the parallel resistance differ from 30 Ω?
impedance.hint: Q = |X|/R = 4/3. Use $R_p$ = R(1 + Q²) and $X_p$ = X(1 + 1/Q²).

solution.text: Both forms must have the same admittance.

solution.answer: 83.3 Ω in parallel with 9.95 mH. Conductance is the real part of $1/Z$, which depends on X as well as R.

impedance.title: Same shape, new values
impedance.prompt: An RC low-pass uses 2.2 kΩ and 68 nF. (a) Find its corner. (b) Scale it so the resistor is 22 kΩ without changing the response. (c) Then move the response four times higher in frequency, keeping 22 kΩ.
impedance.hint: Impedance scaling multiplies R by k and divides C by k. Frequency scaling divides C (and L) by the frequency factor.

solution.text: Multiply R by 10 and divide C by 10. RC is unchanged, so the response is unchanged.
Keep R and divide C by 4.
The nearest standard value, 1.8 nF, gives 4.02 kHz.

solution.answer: (a) 1.06 kHz; (b) 22 kΩ + 6.8 nF; (c) 22 kΩ + 1.7 nF (4.26 kHz).

reactive-power.title: Infer the load from three readings
reactive-power.prompt: A 230 V RMS, 50 Hz supply feeds a load drawing 4.0 A RMS. A wattmeter reads 690 W. Find the apparent power, power factor, reactive power and phase angle. If the load is inductive, model it as series R and L.
reactive-power.hint: S = V·I; PF = P/S; Q = √(S² − P²).

solution.answer: 920 VA, PF 0.75, 609 var, θ = 41.4°. Model: 43.1 Ω in series with 121 mH.

reactive-power.title: Current without power
reactive-power.prompt: A 10 µF capacitor is connected across 230 V RMS, 50 Hz. Find the RMS current, the reactive power, the average power, and the peak energy stored. At what frequency does its instantaneous power oscillate?
reactive-power.hint: I = VωC. For an ideal capacitor P = 0 and Q = −V·I.

solution.text: An ideal capacitor dissipates nothing. By convention its reactive power is negative.
The peak voltage is $\sqrt2\times230$ = 325 V.
$p(t)=v(t)i(t)$ is a product of two 50 Hz sinusoids 90° apart, so it oscillates at twice the line frequency.

solution.answer: 0.723 A, −166 var, 0 W, 0.53 J peak; power oscillates at 100 Hz.

reactive-power.title: Correct a motor to 0.95
reactive-power.prompt: A single-phase 400 V RMS, 50 Hz motor takes 5 kW at PF 0.80 lagging. Find the capacitance needed to raise the PF to 0.95 lagging and the line current before and after.
reactive-power.hint: Q = P tan $\theta$. The capacitor must supply the difference in Q.

solution.text: A capacitor across V supplies $Q=\omega CV^2$.

solution.answer: About 42 µF; line current falls from 15.6 A to 13.2 A.

reactive-power.title: Conjugate or resistive?
reactive-power.prompt: A 2 V RMS source has internal impedance 75 − 40j Ω. Find the load giving maximum power and that power. Then find the best purely resistive load and its power.
reactive-power.hint: Conjugate match gives |V|²/(4R_s). For a resistive load, maximize I²$R_L$ with I = V/|$Z_s$ + $R_L$|; the optimum is $R_L$ = |$Z_s$|.

solution.text: Maximum power needs $Z_L=Z_s^*$, which cancels the reactance and leaves $2R_s$ in the loop.
Maximizing $I^2R_L$ with a fixed source reactance gives $R_L=|Z_s|$.

solution.answer: Conjugate: 75 + 40j Ω, 13.3 mW. Resistive: 85 Ω, 12.5 mW (6% less).

reactive-power.title: A factor of two hiding in a phasor
reactive-power.prompt: A student uses peak phasors, V = 10∠0° V across a 50 Ω resistor, and computes S = V I* = 10 × 0.2 = 2 W. A thermometer suggests the resistor dissipates half that. Who is right, and why?
reactive-power.hint: What is the RMS value of a 10 V peak sinusoid?

solution.text: Average power from peak amplitudes carries a factor of ½.

solution.answer: The thermometer is right: 1 W. $S=VI^*$ assumes RMS phasors.

rc-filters.title: A 2 kHz low-pass
rc-filters.prompt: Design an RC low-pass with a −3 dB frequency near 2 kHz using R = 4.7 kΩ. Choose a standard capacitor from 10, 15, 22, 33… nF and find the resulting corner, and the gain and phase at 20 kHz.

solution.text: 15 nF gives a corner above 2 kHz, 22 nF below. Take 15 nF.

solution.answer: 15 nF → corner 2.26 kHz; at 20 kHz, −19.0 dB and −83.6°.

rc-filters.title: Add, don’t multiply
rc-filters.prompt: A signal passes through an amplifier with voltage gain 20, an attenuator of 0.25, and a filter at its −3 dB point. Find the overall gain in dB and as a ratio.
rc-filters.hint: Convert each stage to dB with 20 log₁₀, then add.

solution.answer: +10.97 dB, a ratio of 3.54.

rc-filters.title: How much does the coupling capacitor cost?
rc-filters.prompt: A 4.7 µF coupling capacitor feeds a 2.2 kΩ input. Find the corner frequency, and the gain (in dB) and phase at 50 Hz and at 15 Hz.
rc-filters.hint: It is a high-pass: |H| = x/√(1 + x²), ∠H = 90° − tan⁻¹ x, with x = f/f₃dB.

solution.answer: Corner 15.4 Hz. At 50 Hz: −0.39 dB, +17.1°. At 15 Hz: −3.12 dB, +45.7°.

rc-filters.title: A filter between a source and a load
rc-filters.prompt: A 10 kΩ / 22 nF low-pass is driven by a source with 600 Ω output resistance and loaded by 47 kΩ. Find the DC gain and the −3 dB frequency, and compare with the ideal 10 kΩ / 22 nF corner.
rc-filters.hint: Add the source resistance to R. Then find the Thévenin resistance seen by the capacitor.

solution.text: At DC the capacitor is open; the source resistance, 10 kΩ and load form a divider.
Short the source; the capacitor sees 10.6 kΩ in parallel with 47 kΩ.

solution.answer: DC gain 0.816 (−1.77 dB), corner 836 Hz instead of 723 Hz.

rc-filters.title: Two ways to the same triangle
rc-filters.prompt: A ±2 V, 1 kHz square wave drives a 100 kΩ / 100 nF low-pass. Estimate the peak-to-peak triangle at the output using the time domain. Then check your answer with the square wave’s fundamental.
rc-filters.hint: The corner is far below 1 kHz, so the output barely moves and the capacitor current is about ±V/R. The fundamental of a square wave of amplitude A is 4A/π; a triangle of amplitude B has fundamental 8B/π².

solution.text: The corner is far below 1 kHz, so the output stays near 0 V and the resistor sees about ±2 V.
The square wave's fundamental is $4A/\pi$ = 2.55 V. The filter attenuates 1 kHz by about 15.9/1000.
A triangle of amplitude 50 mV has fundamental $(8/\pi^2)(50\ \text{mV})$ = 40.5 mV, which agrees.

solution.answer: About 0.10 V p-p (50 mV amplitude); both methods agree.

poles.title: Count the poles
poles.prompt: A low-pass response measures −20 dB at 10 kHz and −56 dB at 40 kHz, both well above its corners. Approximately how many poles does it have?
poles.hint: 40 kHz is two octaves above 10 kHz.

solution.text: 10 kHz → 20 kHz → 40 kHz is two octaves.

solution.step: Divide by the slope per pole
solution.text: Each pole gives 6 dB/octave (20 dB/decade).

solution.answer: Three poles (−60 dB/decade).

poles.title: Three buffered sections
poles.prompt: Three buffered identical RC low-pass sections each have their corner at 1 kHz. Find the gain and phase at 1 kHz, the overall −3 dB frequency, and the gain at 10 kHz.
poles.hint: Gains in dB and phases add. For n identical poles the −3 dB point is $f_c$√(2^(1/n) − 1).

solution.text: Each section is at its corner: −3.01 dB and −45°.
Solve $(1+x^2)^{3/2}=\sqrt2$ for $x=f/f_c$.

solution.answer: At 1 kHz: −9.03 dB, −135°. −3 dB at 510 Hz. At 10 kHz: −60.1 dB.

poles.title: Two sections, no buffer
poles.prompt: Two identical 10 kΩ / 10 nF low-pass sections are connected directly. Find the two pole frequencies and the gain at 1.59 kHz. How could you reduce the interaction without an amplifier?
poles.hint: With x = ωRC the response is 1/(1 − x² + 3jx). Its denominator factors with roots x = (3 ± √5)/2.

solution.text: With $x=\omega RC$, nodal analysis of the two unbuffered sections gives
In terms of $s\tau$: $s^2\tau^2+3s\tau+1=0$ has roots $s\tau=-(3\pm\sqrt5)/2$ = −0.382 and −2.618.
Scale the second section's impedance up: 100 kΩ with 1 nF keeps RC but loads the first section ten times less, bringing the gain at $x$ = 1 to about −6.4 dB.

solution.answer: Poles at 608 Hz and 4.17 kHz; gain −9.54 dB at 1.59 kHz (vs −6.02 dB buffered). Use a higher-impedance second section.

poles.title: 100 Hz to 10 kHz
poles.prompt: Design a buffered RC band-pass with corners at 100 Hz and 10 kHz, using 10 kΩ in both sections. Find both capacitors, the center frequency, and the gains at the center and at 100 Hz.
poles.hint: Each section is designed separately because the buffer isolates them.

solution.text: The geometric mean of the corners.
Each section is a decade from its corner: $20\log(1/\sqrt{1.01})$ = −0.04 dB.
The high-pass is at its corner (−3.01 dB); the low-pass is two decades below its corner (≈ 0 dB).

solution.answer: $C_1$ = 159 nF, $C_2$ = 1.59 nF, centre 1 kHz at −0.09 dB, −3.01 dB at 100 Hz.

poles.title: A 50 Hz twin-T
poles.prompt: Design a twin-T notch for 50 Hz with C = 47 nF. List all four component values and find the attenuation at 150 Hz and 100 Hz.
poles.hint: $f_0$ = 1/(2πRC). The T’s use R, R, 2C and C, C, R/2. For the ideal twin-T, H = (1 − x²)/(1 − x² + 4jx).

solution.text: One T uses R, R and 2C; the other uses C, C and R/2.

solution.answer: 67.7 kΩ, 33.9 kΩ, 47 nF, 94 nF. −5.1 dB at 150 Hz and −9.1 dB at 100 Hz: deep at 50 Hz but broad (Q = ¼).

resonance.title: An RF series resonator
resonance.prompt: A series circuit has L = 47 µH, C = 220 pF and R = 12 Ω. Find $f_0$, $Z_0$, Q and the half-power bandwidth.

solution.answer: $f_0$ = 1.565 MHz, $Z_0$ = 462 Ω, Q = 38.5, B = 40.6 kHz.

resonance.title: How many volts on the capacitor?
resonance.prompt: The circuit of the previous problem is driven at $f_0$ by 0.5 V. Find the current and the capacitor voltage. What capacitor voltage rating would you specify?
resonance.hint: At resonance Z = R, and |$V_C$| = I $Z_0$ = Q V.

solution.text: The reactances cancel, leaving R = 12 Ω.
Allow margin for higher drive or Q: at least 25 V.

solution.answer: 41.7 mA; the capacitor sees 19.3 V, 38.5× the drive. Specify ≥ 25 V.

resonance.title: Loading a tank
resonance.prompt: A parallel tank uses 330 µH (winding resistance 8 Ω) and 470 pF. Find $f_0$, Q and the impedance at resonance. A 47 kΩ load is connected across it: find the new effective Q and bandwidth.
resonance.hint: Unloaded: Z ≈ L/(rC). Loaded: combine in parallel with 47 kΩ, then Q = $R_{parallel}$/$Z_0$.

solution.text: The series loss transforms to a large parallel resistance.

solution.answer: $f_0$ = 404 kHz, Q = 105, $Z$ = 87.8 kΩ. Loaded: Q = 36.5, B = 11.1 kHz.

resonance.title: A Butterworth LC into 8 Ω
resonance.prompt: Design an LC low-pass with a 2 kHz natural frequency and a flat (Butterworth, Q = 0.707) response into an 8 Ω load, driven from a source with negligible resistance. Find L, C and the attenuation at 20 kHz.
resonance.hint: With $R_s$ ≈ 0, Q = $R_L$/$Z_0$. Then L = $Z_0$/$\omega$₀ and C = 1/($\omega$₀$Z_0$).

solution.text: With a stiff source, the load sets the damping and $Q=R_L/Z_0$.
A two-pole Butterworth falls as $1/\sqrt{1+(f/f_0)^4}$.

solution.answer: L = 0.90 mH, C = 7.0 µF; −40 dB at 20 kHz.

resonance.title: From peaking to overshoot
resonance.prompt: A lightly loaded LC supply filter has Q = 4. Estimate its step-response overshoot. If $Z_0$ = 2 Ω and the load is very light, what added series resistance would bring Q to 0.707?
resonance.hint: ζ = 1/(2Q); overshoot = exp(−πζ/√(1 − ζ²)). With a light load, the series Q is $Z_0$/R.

solution.text: A 5 V step would peak near 5 × 1.67 = 8.4 V.
With a light load the series Q is $Z_0/R$.
2.8 Ω drops 2.8 V per ampere. A parallel R–C damping branch avoids this DC loss.

solution.answer: Overshoot ≈ 67%. About 2.8 Ω of series resistance brings Q to 0.707.

ac-thevenin.title: A high-pass at one frequency
ac-thevenin.prompt: A 1 V source drives a 10 nF series capacitor and a 10 kΩ resistor to ground (a high-pass). At 1 kHz find $V_{\mathrm{th}}$ and $Z_{\mathrm{th}}$ at the output, then the output with a 10 kΩ load.

solution.text: Short the source: R in parallel with $Z_C$.

solution.answer: $V_{th}$ = 0.532∠57.9°, $Z_{th}$ = 7.17 − 4.50j kΩ; loaded output 0.300∠72.6°.

ac-thevenin.title: How big, and how close?
ac-thevenin.prompt: A chip draws 200 mA bursts lasting 20 ns, and its supply may droop by at most 50 mV. Find the minimum local bypass capacitance. If the capacitor’s mounting adds 1 nH and the current rises in 2 ns, what voltage appears across that inductance?
ac-thevenin.hint: ΔV = IΔt/C and v = L di/dt.

solution.text: 0.1 V is twice the whole droop budget. Reducing mounting inductance (short vias, several parallel capacitors) matters more than adding capacitance.

solution.answer: At least 80 nF (use 100 nF). The 1 nH mounting adds 0.1 V, exceeding the budget on its own.

ac-thevenin.title: Ride through a dropout
ac-thevenin.prompt: A 3.3 V LDO with 0.3 V dropout is fed from a 5 V rail and draws 300 mA. How much capacitance on the 5 V rail keeps the regulator in regulation for 5 ms after the 5 V source disappears?
ac-thevenin.hint: The LDO keeps regulating until its input falls to 3.6 V. Use C = IΔt/ΔV.

solution.answer: About 1.07 mF; use 1.5 mF for tolerance and ESR.

ac-thevenin.title: A quiet reference, and its cost
ac-thevenin.prompt: Two 47 kΩ resistors make a 2.5 V reference from a 5 V supply that carries 120 Hz ripple. Size a capacitor from the reference to ground so that ripple is attenuated a further 40 dB beyond the divider’s own halving. How long does the reference take to settle within 1% at power-up?
ac-thevenin.hint: The capacitor sees the divider’s Thévenin resistance. 40 dB is a factor of 100, so the corner must be at most 1.2 Hz.

solution.text: 40 dB is a factor of 100, so the corner must be at most 120/100 = 1.2 Hz.

solution.answer: At least 5.6 µF; it settles to 1% in about 0.6 s (1.1 s with 10 µF).

ac-thevenin.title: Selectivity and loading
ac-thevenin.prompt: An AM tuning tank uses 220 µH. Find the capacitance for 1.2 MHz. What Q gives a 10 kHz bandwidth, and what parallel resistance does that require? If the detector loads the tank with 50 kΩ, what bandwidth results?
ac-thevenin.hint: C = 1/($\omega$₀²L); Q = $f_0$/B; $R_p$ = Q·$Z_0$. A load in parallel lowers $R_p$ and thus Q.

solution.answer: 80 pF, Q = 120, $R_p$ = 199 kΩ. Loaded by 50 kΩ, bandwidth grows to ≈ 50 kHz.

transistor-physics.title: Is the base short?
transistor-physics.prompt: Electrons in a transistor base have $D_n$ = 25 cm²/s and lifetime $\tau_n$ = 0.5 µs. Find the diffusion length. Is a 1 µm base “short,” and what does that imply about the electron profile?
transistor-physics.hint: L = √(Dτ). Convert cm² to µm² carefully: 1 cm² = 10⁸ µm².

solution.text: $L_n=\sqrt{D_n\tau_n}$. Keep the units consistent.
1 cm = 10⁴ µm, so $L_n$ = 35.4 µm.
$W/L_n$ = 1/35.4. Recombination barely acts during the crossing.
With negligible recombination the diffusion current is the same at every depth, so the electron density falls linearly from emitter edge to collector edge.

solution.answer: $L_n$ ≈ 35 µm. A 1 µm base is short: the electron profile is nearly a straight line, and transport loss is only 0.04%.

transistor-physics.title: From geometry to I_S
transistor-physics.prompt: An NPN has emitter area 500 µm², base doping 5 × 10¹⁶ cm⁻³, neutral base width 1 µm and $D_n$ = 20 cm²/s, with $n_i$ = 10¹⁰ cm⁻³. Estimate $I_S$ and the collector current at $V_{BE}$ = 0.70 V ($V_T$ = 25.85 mV).
transistor-physics.hint: $I_S$ = qAD_n $n_i$²/($N_A$ W). Work in SI: 500 µm² = 5 × 10⁻¹⁰ m², 5 × 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ = 5 × 10²² m⁻³.

solution.text: $I_S$ is proportional to area and inversely proportional to doping and base width. Doubling $I_S$ lowers $V_{BE}$ at fixed current by $V_T\ln2$ = 18 mV.

solution.answer: $I_S$ ≈ 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁶ A; $I_C$ ≈ 0.18 mA at 0.70 V.

transistor-physics.title: Two loss terms
transistor-physics.prompt: In a transistor, the back-injection term D_pN_AW/(D_nN_EW_E) is 0.004 and the base transport term W²/(2L_n²) is 0.0015. Find $\beta$, $\gamma$, $\alpha_T$ and $\alpha$. Which change would raise $\beta$ more: halving the first term or halving the second?
transistor-physics.hint: 1/$\beta$ is the sum of the two terms.

solution.text: The two loss terms add to give $1/\beta$.

solution.answer: β ≈ 182, γ = 0.996, $\alpha_T$ = 0.9985, α = 0.9945. Halving the back-injection term helps more (β → 286).

transistor-physics.title: Estimate V_A from base width
transistor-physics.prompt: As $V_{CB}$ rises from 0 to 5 V, a transistor’s neutral base width falls from 0.70 µm to 0.65 µm while $V_{BE}$ is held fixed. Estimate the change in collector current and the Early voltage.
transistor-physics.hint: $I_C$ ∝ 1/W at fixed edge density. Extrapolate the straight line I_C(V) back to zero current.

solution.text: At fixed $V_{BE}$ the edge density is fixed, and the diffusion current scales as $1/W$.
7.7% over 5 V is 1.54% per volt of the 0 V current.
The line $I_C=I_0(1+0.0154V_{CB})$ reaches zero at $V_{CB}=-1/0.0154$.

solution.answer: $I_C$ rises 7.7%; $V_A$ ≈ 65 V.

transistor-physics.title: A warm transistor at fixed V_BE
transistor-physics.prompt: A transistor carries 1 mA with $V_{BE}$ = 0.650 V at 25 °C. Estimate $V_{BE}$ at 85 °C for the same current. If instead $V_{BE}$ were held at 0.650 V, roughly how much would the current rise per degree, and over the full 60 °C?
transistor-physics.hint: Use −2.1 mV/°C. At fixed $V_{BE}$, a 2.1 mV equivalent change in a 25.85 mV exponential scale is a fractional change.

solution.text: A 2.1 mV/°C shift is equivalent to raising $V_{BE}$ by 2.1 mV at fixed temperature, and $I_C\propto e^{V_{BE}/V_T}$.
The equivalent change is 126 mV. Use $V_T$ at 85 °C, 31 mV.

solution.answer: 0.524 V at fixed current. At fixed $V_{BE}$ the current rises about 8%/°C, roughly 60× over 60 °C.

bjt.title: Split the emitter current
bjt.prompt: A transistor with $\beta$ = 150 carries 3.0 mA of emitter current. Find $I_B$, $I_C$ and $\alpha$.

solution.answer: $I_B$ = 19.9 µA, $I_C$ = 2.98 mA, α = 0.9934.

bjt.title: A solenoid from a 3.3 V pin
bjt.prompt: A 24 V, 250 mA solenoid (with a flywheel diode) must be switched by a 3.3 V logic output that can supply at most 8 mA. The NPN has $\beta$ ≥ 40. Design for a forced $\beta$ of 10. What base resistor is needed, and is the design feasible? Suggest an alternative.

solution.text: Forced β = 10 means the base current is a tenth of the collector current.
The pin can supply 8 mA, a third of what is needed. Even with no overdrive, 250/40 = 6.3 mA leaves no margin.
A Darlington pair (β in the thousands), a two-transistor driver, or a logic-level MOSFET, whose gate needs no steady current.

solution.answer: Needs 25 mA through ≈ 100 Ω: not feasible from an 8 mA pin. Use a logic-level MOSFET or a Darlington.

bjt.title: Size both resistors
bjt.prompt: Drive a 2.0 V, 15 mA LED from 5 V with a transistor whose $V_{CE(\mathrm{sat})}$ is 0.15 V and minimum $\beta$ is 100. Use fivefold overdrive and a 5 V logic signal. Choose standard values.
bjt.hint: Collector resistor from the voltage left after the LED and $V_{CE(\mathrm{sat})}$.

solution.answer: R_C = 180 Ω (15.8 mA), R_B = 5.1 kΩ (about 0.84 mA from the logic pin).

bjt.title: Which region?
bjt.prompt: Measured on a working NPN circuit (all to ground): (a) $V_B$ = 2.00 V, $V_E$ = 1.35 V, $V_C$ = 7.2 V; (b) $V_B$ = 2.00 V, $V_E$ = 1.35 V, $V_C$ = 1.45 V; (c) $V_B$ = 0.30 V, $V_E$ = 0 V, $V_C$ = 12 V. Identify the region in each case.
bjt.hint: Check whether the base–emitter junction is on, then whether the base–collector junction is forward-biased.

solution.text: $V_{BE}$ = 0.30 V is far below the ~0.6 V needed for significant current, and the collector sits at the supply because no current flows through its resistor.

solution.answer: (a) active; (b) saturated; (c) cut off.

bjt.title: A PNP switch and its base resistor
bjt.prompt: A PNP transistor switches a 0.5 A grounded load from 12 V. Its minimum $\beta$ is 50; use twofold overdrive. A small NPN pulls the PNP’s base toward ground ($V_{CE(\mathrm{sat})}$ = 0.1 V); take the PNP’s $V_{EB}$ as 0.8 V at this current. Find the base resistor and its dissipation. Why add a resistor from PNP base to emitter?

solution.text: From the 12 V supply: subtract $V_{EB}$ and the NPN's saturation voltage.
When the NPN turns off, a few kilohms from base to emitter removes stored base charge and holds the PNP off against leakage.

solution.answer: 560 Ω, dissipating about 0.22 W (use ≥ ¼ W). The base–emitter resistor gives fast, reliable turn-off.

emitter-follower.title: Looking in, looking back
emitter-follower.prompt: A follower with $\beta$ = 150 has $R_E$ = 2.2 kΩ and drives a 2.2 kΩ load (AC-coupled). Its base is driven from a 47 kΩ source. Ignoring $r_e$, find $Z_{\mathrm{in}}$ at the base and $Z_{\mathrm{out}}$ at the emitter. How much does $r_e$ ≈ 26 Ω (at 1 mA) change $Z_{\mathrm{out}}$?
emitter-follower.hint: Signal resistance in the emitter is $R_E$ ∥ $R_L$.

solution.text: Looking into the emitter, the source resistance is divided by β + 1.

solution.answer: $Z_{in}$ ≈ 166 kΩ, $Z_{out}$ ≈ 311 Ω (337 Ω with $r_e$, an 8% change).

emitter-follower.title: Can it pull down far enough?
emitter-follower.prompt: A DC-coupled follower runs from ±12 V with $R_E$ = 3.3 kΩ to −12 V, driving 1 kΩ to ground. What is the most negative output? What $R_E$ allows a swing to −6 V, and what standing current does that imply at 0 V output?
emitter-follower.hint: With the transistor off, $R_E$ and $R_L$ form a divider from −12 V.

solution.text: When the transistor cuts off, $R_E$ and $R_L$ divide −12 V.
At −6 V the load draws 6 mA from ground, which $R_E$ must carry with only 6 V across it.

solution.answer: Floor −2.79 V. For −6 V need $R_E$ ≤ 1 kΩ, costing 12 mA standing current.

emitter-follower.title: Size the zener resistor
emitter-follower.prompt: Design a zener-plus-follower regulator for 100 mA from an input that varies from 13 V to 16 V, using a 10 V zener that needs at least 5 mA. Transistor $\beta$ ≥ 50. Find R, the output voltage, and the transistor’s dissipation at the highest input.
emitter-follower.hint: The worst case for the resistor is minimum input with maximum base current.

solution.text: Minimum input, full load: R must supply the base current plus 5 mA for the zener.

solution.answer: R = 390 Ω, output 9.35 V, transistor dissipates 0.67 W at 16 V input.

emitter-follower.title: A follower driving a big capacitor
emitter-follower.prompt: A follower charges a 10 µF capacitor to +8 V. Its base is then suddenly driven to −5 V. What happens to the base–emitter junction, and how would you protect it?
emitter-follower.hint: The capacitor holds the emitter voltage while the base moves.

solution.text: 10 µF cannot discharge instantly, so the emitter stays near +8 V.
13 V exceeds a typical $V_{EBO}$ of about 6 V, so the junction avalanches. That permanently degrades β.
Put a diode across the base–emitter junction (anode at emitter, cathode at base) so the capacitor discharges into the driver; a base resistor limits that current.

solution.answer: The junction sees 13 V reverse and breaks down. Add a reverse diode across B–E.

emitter-follower.title: When a follower is not enough
emitter-follower.prompt: A 1 V signal with 50 kΩ source resistance must drive 470 Ω. Compare a direct connection with a follower biased at 1 mA, $R_E$ = 1 kΩ (signal resistance $R_E$ ∥ $R_L$ = 320 Ω), $\beta$ = 100. Include $r_e$. What limits the follower here?
emitter-follower.hint: $Z_{\mathrm{in}}$ = ($\beta$ + 1)($r_e$ + $R_E$ ∥ $R_L$). Then two dividers: source into $Z_{\mathrm{in}}$, and the follower’s internal $r_e$ into 320 Ω.

solution.text: $(\beta+1)\times320$ Ω is still less than the 50 kΩ source. More gain in impedance, from a Darlington or higher β, is needed.

solution.answer: Direct: 9.3 mV. Follower: 0.38 V, 40× better, but still limited by $(\beta+1)R$ < 50 kΩ.

bjt-biasing.title: Bias a 2 mA follower on 12 V
bjt-biasing.prompt: Design the bias for an emitter follower on 12 V with about 2 mA quiescent and the emitter near mid-supply. Minimum $\beta$ is 80. Use $R_1$ = 39 kΩ (top) and $R_2$ = 47 kΩ (bottom); check the stiffness rule and find the actual emitter current and the input impedance.

solution.answer: $R_E$ = 3 kΩ; the divider passes the rule; $I_E$ = 1.81 mA ($V_E$ = 5.43 V); $Z_{in}$ = 19.6 kΩ.

bjt-biasing.title: How much does β matter?
bjt-biasing.prompt: A common-emitter stage on 12 V uses a 56 kΩ / 10 kΩ divider and $R_E$ = 1 kΩ. Find $I_C$ for $\beta$ = 80 and $\beta$ = 400.

solution.answer: 1.04 mA and 1.14 mA: a 5× change in β moves the current by only 9%.

bjt-biasing.title: Why a volt across R_E?
bjt-biasing.prompt: Compare two bias designs with the same current, one with $V_E$ = 0.5 V and one with $V_E$ = 2.0 V. Estimate the fractional current change for a 50 °C temperature rise in each.

solution.text: With the base voltage fixed, $V_E$ rises by 105 mV, and $I\propto V_E$.

solution.answer: +21% with $V_E$ = 0.5 V, +5.3% with $V_E$ = 2.0 V.

bjt-biasing.title: The single base resistor
bjt-biasing.prompt: A stage on 12 V uses a single 1 MΩ base resistor and $R_C$ = 4.7 kΩ, emitter grounded. Find $I_C$ and $V_C$ for $\beta$ = 80 and $\beta$ = 400.
bjt-biasing.hint: $I_B$ = (12 − 0.65)/1 MΩ; check whether $V_C$ goes below about 0.2 V.

solution.text: It does not depend on β.

solution.answer: β = 80: 0.91 mA, 7.7 V. β = 400: saturated at ≈ 2.5 mA, 0.2 V. Single-resistor bias depends entirely on β.

bjt-biasing.title: Input capacitor for the audio follower
bjt-biasing.prompt: The audio follower of the chapter has $Z_{\mathrm{in}}$ = 63.8 kΩ. What low-frequency corner does a 0.1 µF input capacitor give? What value puts the corner at 2 Hz?

solution.text: Round up: 1.5 µF or 2.2 µF. A film capacitor avoids polarity concerns.

solution.answer: 0.1 µF gives 25 Hz; use 1.5–2.2 µF for a 2 Hz corner.

bjt-small-signal.title: Four numbers from one current
bjt-small-signal.prompt: A transistor runs at $I_C$ = 0.2 mA with $\beta$ = 150 and $V_A$ = 80 V. Find $g_m$, $r_e$, r_π and $r_o$.

solution.answer: $g_m$ = 7.74 mS, $r_e$ = 129 Ω, $r_\pi$ = 19.4 kΩ, $r_o$ = 400 kΩ.

bjt-small-signal.title: Into the base with degeneration
bjt-small-signal.prompt: At 2 mA, with $\beta$ = 120 and 470 Ω in the emitter, what impedance looks into the base? What fraction of that is due to $r_e$?

solution.answer: 58.4 kΩ; $r_e$ contributes only about 2.7%.

bjt-small-signal.title: Follower output impedance
bjt-small-signal.prompt: A follower biased at 0.5 mA is driven from 4.7 kΩ, $\beta$ = 100. Find the output impedance looking into the emitter.

solution.answer: ≈ 98 Ω. At this current $r_e$ is as large as the source term, so raising the bias current helps most.

bjt-small-signal.title: How small is small enough?
bjt-small-signal.prompt: For what base–emitter signal amplitude is the small-signal model’s peak current error about 5%?
bjt-small-signal.hint: The error relative to the linear term is approximately v/(2V_T).

solution.step: Ratio of quadratic to linear term

solution.answer: About 2.6 mV peak at the base–emitter junction.

bjt-small-signal.title: A common-emitter gain by small-signal analysis
bjt-small-signal.prompt: A stage runs at 2 mA with $R_C$ = 3.3 kΩ and 220 Ω unbypassed in the emitter. Find the small-signal voltage gain.

solution.text: The collector current is set by the total emitter resistance; the output voltage is that current times $R_C$.
Ignoring $r_e$ gives −3300/220 = −15.0.

solution.answer: G ≈ −14.2.

current-sources.title: A 2 mA sink
current-sources.prompt: Design a 2 mA current sink on 12 V with the base held at 2.65 V by a stiff divider. Find $R_E$ and the largest load resistance it can drive.

solution.text: The collector may fall to $V_E$ + 0.2 V before saturating.

solution.answer: $R_E$ = 1 kΩ; load up to 4.9 kΩ.

current-sources.title: Source current into a grounded load
current-sources.prompt: A PNP source has its emitter resistor of 2.2 kΩ to +15 V and its base held 3.3 V below the supply by a zener. Find the output current and the largest grounded load it can drive.
current-sources.hint: The emitter sits one $V_{BE}$ above the base, i.e. 3.3 − 0.65 V below the supply.

solution.text: The collector can rise to 0.2 V below the emitter.

solution.answer: 1.20 mA into loads up to about 10 kΩ.

current-sources.title: Drift and its cure
current-sources.prompt: A current source has $V_E$ = 1.0 V. Estimate its current change over a 60 °C rise. How does putting a diode in series with the lower divider resistor help?

solution.text: The diode in the divider lowers the base voltage by about 2 mV/°C as it warms, tracking $V_{BE}$. $V_E=V_B-V_{BE}$ then stays nearly constant.

solution.answer: About +12.6%. The diode cancels most of the drift; what remains is junction mismatch.

current-sources.title: How good is the source?
current-sources.prompt: A source runs at 0.5 mA with $V_A$ = 60 V, $\beta$ = 150 and $R_E$ = 2 kΩ. Estimate its output resistance, and compare with $r_o$ alone and with the $\beta r_o$ limit.

solution.step: Emitter resistance in parallel with r_π

solution.text: 32× $r_o$, and below the $\beta r_o$ = 18 MΩ ceiling. A 5 V load change moves the current by 5/3.8 MΩ ≈ 1.3 µA.

solution.answer: $R_{out}$ ≈ 3.8 MΩ (vs 120 kΩ for $r_o$ alone; limit 18 MΩ).

current-sources.title: A linear sweep
current-sources.prompt: A 0.5 mA current source charges a 0.22 µF capacitor connected from its collector to the supply (so the capacitor voltage grows as the collector falls). Find the ramp rate and the time to sweep 10 V. What sets the end of the linear ramp?

solution.text: The ramp stays linear until the collector falls to $V_E$ + 0.2 V; then the transistor saturates and the current collapses.

solution.answer: 2.27 V/ms; 10 V in 4.4 ms. Compliance ends the ramp.

common-emitter.title: First model and refinement
common-emitter.prompt: A stage has $R_C$ = 10 kΩ, $R_E$ = 1.5 kΩ (unbypassed) and $I_C$ = 0.6 mA. Find the gain from the first model and with $r_e$.

solution.answer: −6.67 (first model), −6.48 with $r_e$.

common-emitter.title: The bypassed limit
common-emitter.prompt: A bypassed stage has 5 V across its collector resistor. What is its maximum small-signal gain, whatever the current? Why might you not want it?

solution.text: With the emitter at AC ground, $G=-R_C/r_e=-g_mR_C$.
Gain depends on temperature through $V_T$, distortion is large above a few millivolts, and input impedance falls to $(\beta+1)r_e$.

solution.answer: −193, but unstable, nonlinear and low-impedance.

common-emitter.title: Design for a gain of −20
common-emitter.prompt: A stage at 1 mA has $R_C$ = 4.7 kΩ and a total emitter resistance of 1 kΩ for bias. Split $R_E$ to give a gain of −20 with the remainder bypassed.

solution.text: 200 Ω unbypassed and 820 Ω bypassed keep about 1 kΩ total for bias.

solution.answer: 200 Ω unbypassed + 820 Ω bypassed; gain ≈ −20.8.

common-emitter.title: A load halves the gain
common-emitter.prompt: The stage of the previous problem but with 470 Ω unbypassed (gain about −9.5) drives a 4.7 kΩ load. Find the loaded gain and the maximum symmetric output swing set by cutoff at 1 mA.
common-emitter.hint: Signals see $R_C$ ∥ $R_L$; the upward swing is limited to I_CQ($R_C$ ∥ $R_L$).

solution.text: The collector can rise only until the transistor current reaches zero; the 1 mA then flows from $R_C$ into the load.

solution.answer: Loaded gain −4.74; symmetric swing limited to about ±2.35 V.

common-emitter.title: How big must C_E be?
common-emitter.prompt: In the partially bypassed stage (180 Ω unbypassed, 820 Ω bypassed, 1 mA), find the resistance seen by the bypass capacitor and the capacitance for a 20 Hz corner. Neglect source resistance.

solution.text: Looking from the capacitor: 820 Ω in parallel with the path back through 180 Ω and $r_e$.
