Use 100 µF so this corner sits below the coupling-capacitor corners.

solution.answer: 165 Ω; at least 48 µF (use 100 µF).

transconductance.title: Balanced outputs
transconductance.prompt: A phase splitter has $R_C$ = $R_E$ = 3.3 kΩ at 1.5 mA. Find $r_e$ and both gains.

solution.text: The emitter output is a follower: $R_E$ over the total emitter resistance.
The same signal current flows through $R_C$, with the opposite sign.

solution.answer: $r_e$ = 17.2 Ω; gains +0.995 and −0.995.

transconductance.title: One load, two outputs
transconductance.prompt: The splitter of the previous problem has a 3.3 kΩ load connected (through a capacitor) to its collector output only. Find the new collector gain. What happens to the emitter gain?
transconductance.hint: The collector current is unchanged; only the resistance it flows into changes.

solution.text: It is set by the input voltage across $R_E+r_e$; the collector behaves as a current source.
Nothing at the emitter changed, so it stays +0.995.

solution.answer: $G_C$ = −0.497; $G_E$ stays +0.995. The outputs are now unbalanced.

transconductance.title: Balance a known load
transconductance.prompt: A splitter has $R_E$ = 4.7 kΩ, $r_e$ = 28 Ω, and its collector output always drives 10 kΩ. What $R_C$ restores equal gains?
transconductance.hint: Make $R_C$ ∥ 10 kΩ equal to $R_E$ + $r_e$ so that |$G_C$| = 1 — or to $R_E$ for |$G_C$| = $G_E$.

solution.text: $|G_C|=G_E$ requires the total collector load to equal $R_E$.
If instead the collector load equals $R_E+r_e$ = 4.728 kΩ, $|G_C|$ = 1 exactly and $R_C$ = 8.97 kΩ.

solution.answer: $R_C$ ≈ 8.87 kΩ (8.87 kΩ 1% or 9.1 kΩ).

transconductance.title: What degeneration costs
transconductance.prompt: At 2 mA with 470 Ω of emitter degeneration, find the stage transconductance and compare it with $g_m$ of the bare transistor.

solution.answer: $G_m$ = 2.07 mS versus 77.4 mS: degeneration trades 37× transconductance for linearity and predictability.

transconductance.title: Constant amplitude, variable phase
transconductance.prompt: A splitter’s outputs drive R = 10 kΩ (from the collector) and C = 15.9 nF (from the emitter) to a common node. Find the output phase at 100 Hz, 1 kHz and 10 kHz.

solution.text: With equal and opposite drives through R and C, the node voltage has constant amplitude and phase $180^\circ-2\arctan(\omega RC)$.

solution.answer: 168.6°, 90° and 11.4° at 100 Hz, 1 kHz and 10 kHz.

ebers-moll.title: How many millivolts per current?
ebers-moll.prompt: With $I_S$ = 10⁻¹⁴ A at 300 K, find $V_{BE}$ at 1 µA, 1 mA and 10 mA.

solution.answer: 0.476 V, 0.655 V, 0.714 V: 59.5 mV per decade.

ebers-moll.title: Fixed V_BE, rising temperature
ebers-moll.prompt: A transistor with a stiffly fixed $V_{BE}$ (no emitter resistor) warms by 20 °C. Estimate the factor by which its collector current rises.
ebers-moll.hint: Compound 8% per °C, or treat the 42 mV equivalent change in $V_{BE}$ as an exponent.

solution.text: At fixed $V_{BE}$, warming by 20 °C acts like raising $V_{BE}$ by 2.1 × 20 = 42 mV.
Use $V_T$ at about 45 °C: 27.4 mV.

solution.answer: About 4.6–4.7×, enough to risk thermal runaway.

ebers-moll.title: Design and its errors
ebers-moll.prompt: Design a mirror for 0.5 mA on 12 V. With $\beta$ = 80, find the output current. If the output transistor sits at $V_{CE}$ = 8 V and $V_A$ = 75 V, estimate the Early-effect error.

solution.text: Both bases draw from the reference.
$Q_1$ sits at $V_{CE}=V_{BE}$; $Q_2$ at 8 V.

solution.answer: R ≈ 22.7 kΩ; base current gives 0.488 mA (−2.4%); the Early effect adds about +9.8%.

ebers-moll.title: V_CE(sat) from Ebers–Moll
ebers-moll.prompt: A transistor has $\beta_F$ = 200 and $\beta_R$ = 4. Find its ideal $V_{CE(\mathrm{sat})}$ when driven to a forced $\beta$ of 20.

solution.answer: Ideal $V_{CE(sat)}$ ≈ 50 mV; collector resistance adds more in practice.

ebers-moll.title: A 9 V bypassed stage
ebers-moll.prompt: A bypassed common-emitter stage on 9 V has 4 V across its collector resistor. What is its maximum gain? For a 2 mV peak base–emitter signal, by how much do the positive and negative current peaks differ from the linear prediction?
ebers-moll.hint: G = −$V_{RC}$/$V_T$. Peaks scale as e<sup>±v/$V_T$</sup> − 1 compared with v/$V_T$.

solution.text: The peaks are about 4% above and below the linear prediction. The second harmonic is about $v/4V_T$ ≈ 1.9%.

solution.answer: G = −155; peaks +8.04% and −7.45% versus ±7.74%, about 2% second harmonic.

current-mirrors.title: A 200 µA mirror on 5 V
current-mirrors.prompt: Design a basic NPN mirror for 200 µA from a 5 V supply. With $\beta$ = 80, what is the actual output current, ignoring the Early effect?

solution.text: $2/\beta$ = 2.5% low (2.4% exactly).

solution.answer: R ≈ 21.5 kΩ; output ≈ 195 µA.

current-mirrors.title: How good a current source?
current-mirrors.prompt: The mirror of the previous problem drives a load whose voltage is 12 V (on a higher supply rail). The transistors have $V_A$ = 60 V. Estimate the Early-effect error and the output resistance.
current-mirrors.hint: $Q_1$ sits at $V_{CE}$ = $V_{BE}$; $Q_2$ at the output voltage.

solution.text: $Q_1$ is diode-connected at 0.65 V; $Q_2$ sits at 12 V.

solution.answer: About +19% error; $R_{out}$ ≈ 300 kΩ.

current-mirrors.title: Taming mismatch
current-mirrors.prompt: Two discrete transistors in a mirror differ by 2 mV in $V_{BE}$ at equal currents. Compare the current error without emitter resistors and with resistors dropping 0.5 V each.

solution.text: Equal $V_{BE}$ forces currents in the ratio $e^{\Delta V/V_T}$.

Now the base voltages are equal and each emitter loop is $V_{BE}+IR_E$. A 2 mV mismatch must be absorbed by a change in $IR_E$ plus the change in $V_{BE}$, whose incremental slope is $V_T$ per unit fractional current.
The mismatch is now divided by the resistor drop plus $V_T$.

solution.answer: 8.0% without, 0.38% with 0.5 V of degeneration (at the cost of 0.5 V of compliance).

current-mirrors.title: Five microamps from half a milliamp
current-mirrors.prompt: Design a Widlar source giving 5 µA from a 0.5 mA reference. Compare the resistor with the one a basic mirror would need from 15 V.

solution.text: The two $V_{BE}$ values differ by $V_T\ln(I_{ref}/I_{out})$, which appears across $R_E$.

solution.answer: $R_E$ ≈ 23.8 kΩ, versus 2.9 MΩ for a basic mirror.

current-mirrors.title: When is the Wilson worth it?
current-mirrors.prompt: With $\beta$ = 50 and $V_A$ = 100 V at 1 mA, compare the base-current error and output resistance of a basic mirror and a Wilson mirror.

solution.answer: Basic: −3.8%, 100 kΩ. Wilson: 0.077%, 2.5 MΩ, at the cost of one more $V_{BE}$ of headroom.

differential-amplifiers.title: How far does the current move?
differential-amplifiers.prompt: A long-tailed pair has a 2 mA tail. Find both collector currents for a differential input of 20 mV.

solution.answer: 1.37 mA and 0.63 mA: 20 mV already steers 68% of the tail.

differential-amplifiers.title: Differential, common-mode, CMRR
differential-amplifiers.prompt: A pair runs from ±15 V with $R_C$ = 5 kΩ and a 7.15 kΩ tail resistor (2 mA tail). Find the single-ended and differential-output gains, the common-mode gain and the CMRR in dB.
differential-amplifiers.hint: Each side carries 1 mA, so $r_e$ = 25.9 Ω. Use the half circuits.

solution.text: In the differential half circuit the emitters are at AC ground, and each side sees half the input.
Each half carries half the tail current, so it sees $2R_T$ in its emitter.

solution.answer: Single-ended 96.7 (193 differential), $A_{cm}$ = −0.349, CMRR ≈ 49 dB.

differential-amplifiers.title: Trade gain for range
differential-amplifiers.prompt: Add 100 Ω emitter resistors to the pair of the previous problem. Find the new single-ended gain. Why would you do this?

solution.text: The linear input range grows about fivefold, the gain is set by resistors rather than by $I_C$, and the stage is less temperature-sensitive.

solution.answer: Gain falls to 19.9, in exchange for a much wider linear range and stable gain.

differential-amplifiers.title: Gain from the Early voltage
differential-amplifiers.prompt: A pair with a PNP current-mirror load uses transistors with $V_A$ = 80 V (all four). What is the single-ended small-signal gain, independent of the tail current?

solution.text: Each side runs at $I_T/2$; the mirror delivers the full differential current to the output node, which sees $r_{o2}\parallel r_{o4}$.

solution.answer: About 1550, independent of tail current.

differential-amplifiers.title: Where do the millivolts come from?
differential-amplifiers.prompt: The active-loaded stage above (gain 1550) has a 2 mV $V_{BE}$ mismatch. Its inputs are driven from a 10 kΩ source on one side and directly from a low-impedance source on the other; each base draws 5 µA. Estimate the output offset from each cause and suggest a fix for the second.
differential-amplifiers.hint: Bias current × source resistance acts like an input offset voltage.

solution.text: Put 10 kΩ in the other input as well. Equal bias currents then make equal drops that cancel, leaving only offset current × 10 kΩ.

solution.answer: ≈ 3.1 V from mismatch; bias current alone would saturate the output. Balance the source resistances.

push-pull.title: The cost of a single follower
push-pull.prompt: A single NPN follower drives ±12 V into 16 Ω from ±15 V supplies, with its emitter resistor to −15 V. What quiescent current is needed, how much supply power does it draw, and what is the efficiency at full output?
push-pull.hint: The emitter resistor must sink the peak load current at the negative peak.

solution.text: At the negative peak the emitter resistor must sink the whole load current.

solution.answer: 0.75 A, 22.5 W from the supplies, 20% efficient.

push-pull.title: Efficiency and the hottest amplitude
push-pull.prompt: An ideal class B stage runs from ±20 V into 4 Ω. At 16 V peak output, find load power, supply power, efficiency and transistor dissipation. At what amplitude is dissipation greatest, and how much?

solution.text: Each supply delivers half-sine pulses of average $V_p/(\pi R_L)$.
Differentiate $P_D=P_S-P_L$ with respect to $V_p$ and set it to zero.

solution.answer: 32 W, 50.9 W, 62.8%, 18.9 W. Worst at 12.7 V peak, 20.3 W.

push-pull.title: How much of the wave is lost?
push-pull.prompt: A class B stage with a ±0.6 V dead zone is driven by a 2 V peak sine. For what fraction of each cycle is the output essentially zero?

solution.text: There are two zero crossings per cycle, each with 17.5° on either side.

solution.answer: About 19% of each cycle is lost.

push-pull.title: A V_BE multiplier for Darlington outputs
push-pull.prompt: An output stage uses Darlington drivers on both sides, so the bias must span four base–emitter drops of about 0.65 V each. Design a $V_{BE}$ multiplier and find its temperature coefficient.

solution.text: $R_1$ = 1 kΩ, $R_2$ = 3 kΩ, with a trimmer to set the idle current.
The output scales with $V_{BE}$, so its tempco is 4× that of one junction.

solution.answer: $R_2/R_1$ = 3 (e.g. 1 kΩ / 3 kΩ); tempco −8.4 mV/°C.

push-pull.title: Current limit and the short-circuit dilemma
push-pull.prompt: An output stage limits current with a 0.33 Ω emitter resistor and a sensing transistor that turns on at 0.6 V. What is the current limit? With the output shorted, what does the conducting output transistor dissipate on ±15 V supplies?
push-pull.hint: The sensing transistor clamps the drop across the resistor.

solution.step: Voltage across the transistor when shorted
solution.text: Output at 0 V, collector at 15 V: about 15 V across it.

solution.answer: Limit 1.8 A; shorted dissipation ≈ 27 W. Use foldback or thermal shutdown.

darlington.title: Composite β
darlington.prompt: A Darlington uses $\beta$₁ = 100 and $\beta$₂ = 40. Find the composite current gain and the base current needed for 2 A in the active region.

solution.text: $Q_1$ carries $I_{B2}$ = 2 A/41 ≈ 49 mA, which it can supply with only 0.49 mA of base current.

solution.answer: β ≈ 4140; 0.48 mA of base current.

darlington.title: Input impedance
darlington.prompt: That Darlington is used as an emitter follower driving an 8 Ω load. Ignoring $r_e$, what impedance does its input present?
darlington.hint: Multiply the load by the composite ($\beta$ + 1).

solution.text: A source of a few kilohms can drive the loudspeaker through it.

solution.answer: About 33 kΩ.

darlington.title: The cost of the extra V_BE
darlington.prompt: A load draws 3 A through a saturated switch. Compare dissipation for a Darlington at $V_{CE}$ = 0.9 V and a single hard-driven transistor at 0.2 V. What base drive does the single transistor need with $\beta$ = 30 and twofold overdrive?

solution.answer: Darlington 2.7 W; single 0.6 W but it needs 0.2 A of base drive.

darlington.title: Why the resistor across the output base
darlington.prompt: A Darlington’s driver leaks 1 µA at high temperature, and the output transistor has $\beta$ = 40. Without a bleeder, how much collector current flows when the pair should be off? What does a 1 kΩ bleeder from $Q_2$’s base to emitter do?

solution.text: $Q_1$'s 1 µA leakage flows into $Q_2$'s base.
1 mV is far below turn-on, so $Q_2$ stays off. The resistor also removes $Q_2$'s stored base charge at turn-off.

solution.answer: About 40 µA leaks through without a bleeder; with 1 kΩ, $Q_2$ sees only 1 mV and stays off.

darlington.title: Thermal stability of the bias
darlington.prompt: An output stage’s bias network must track the input $V_{BE}$ of its output devices. Compare the temperature coefficient of the input voltage of a Darlington and of a Sziklai pair.
darlington.hint: Count how many junctions lie between the input terminal and the output emitter.

solution.text: Two junctions in series from input to output emitter.
Only the driver's junction lies in the input path.
In the Darlington, one junction is in the hot output device. In the Sziklai, the driver dissipates little.

solution.answer: Darlington ≈ −4.2 mV/°C; Sziklai ≈ −2.1 mV/°C, from a cooler junction, so it is easier to bias stably.

bootstrapping.title: How big does it look?
bootstrapping.prompt: A 100 kΩ resistor is bootstrapped by a follower with gain 0.98. What is its effective value? What if the gain is 0.995?

solution.text: The resistor sees only $(1-G)$ of the input signal across it, so its current falls by that factor.

solution.answer: 5 MΩ and 20 MΩ.

bootstrapping.title: A driven shield
bootstrapping.prompt: A 1 m cable with 100 pF of capacitance connects a 10 MΩ source to an amplifier. Find the low-pass corner. If the shield is driven by a follower with G = 0.995, what is the new corner?

solution.step: Effective capacitance with a driven shield

solution.answer: 159 Hz unguarded; 32 kHz guarded.

bootstrapping.title: What limits the bootstrapped follower?
bootstrapping.prompt: A bootstrapped follower has $\beta$ = 200, $R_E$ = 4.7 kΩ and a bias divider whose parallel resistance is 47 kΩ, connected to the emitter through the bootstrap capacitor. Estimate the maximum input impedance, ignoring $r_e$ and assuming the bootstrapped $R_3$ is huge.
bootstrapping.hint: The divider now loads the emitter; the base sees ($\beta$ + 1) times the total emitter load.

solution.text: The bootstrap capacitor connects the divider to the emitter, so it loads the emitter.

solution.answer: About 860 kΩ.

bootstrapping.title: Negative gain shrinks impedance
bootstrapping.prompt: A 100 kΩ resistor connects the input and output of an inverting amplifier with gain −9. What resistance does the input see through it? What does this have to do with the Miller effect?

solution.step: Apply the formula with negative gain

solution.text: Impedance falls by 10, so a capacitor looks 10 times larger.
That is the Miller effect: bootstrapping with negative gain.

solution.answer: 10 kΩ; this is the Miller effect.

bootstrapping.title: A bootstrapped collector resistor
bootstrapping.prompt: A common-emitter stage at 1 mA has its collector load split; the 5 kΩ section next to the collector is bootstrapped by a follower with G = 0.98 and input impedance 500 kΩ. The transistor’s $r_o$ is 100 kΩ. Estimate the effective load and the voltage gain.
bootstrapping.hint: The bootstrapped resistor looks R/(1 − G); combine it in parallel with the follower’s input and $r_o$.

solution.answer: Load ≈ 62.5 kΩ; gain ≈ 2400 (versus ~390 with a plain 10 kΩ).

current-sharing.title: An exponential split
current-sharing.prompt: Two paralleled transistors with no ballast share 3 A. One needs 8 mV less $V_{BE}$ than the other at equal current. Ignoring heating, how is the current split?

solution.text: The hotter device would also need less $V_{BE}$, making it worse.

solution.answer: 1.73 A and 1.27 A.

current-sharing.title: Size the resistors
current-sharing.prompt: For the same pair at 1.5 A each, choose emitter resistors that keep the static imbalance below 5%. What does each resistor dissipate?

solution.answer: 0.1 Ω, dissipating 0.23 W each.

current-sharing.title: Stable or not?
current-sharing.prompt: Each device carries 1 A at $V_{CE}$ = 20 V on a heat sink giving 3 °C/W per device. Compute the electro-thermal loop gain without ballast and with 0.33 Ω.

solution.text: Each watt raises the junction 3 °C; each degree lowers the needed $V_{BE}$ by 2.1 mV.

solution.answer: 4.9 without ballast (unstable); 0.35 with 0.33 Ω (stable).

current-sharing.title: Minimum ballast for margin
current-sharing.prompt: For the conditions of the previous problem, find the smallest emitter resistor that keeps the loop gain at or below 0.5.

solution.answer: 0.27 Ω (G ≈ 0.43).

current-sharing.title: Do MOSFETs need ballast?
current-sharing.prompt: Paralleled MOSFETs are often said to share current naturally. When is that true, and when is it not?
current-sharing.hint: How does $R_{DS(\mathrm{on})}$ change with temperature, and what happens in linear operation at low gate drive?

solution.text: Fully enhanced, $R_{DS(on)}$ rises with temperature. A hotter device conducts less, which is negative feedback.
Below the zero-temperature-coefficient gate voltage, drain current rises with temperature at fixed $V_{GS}$, which is positive feedback, as in a BJT.
Linear MOSFET stages such as electronic loads still need source resistors or individual control loops.

solution.answer: True when switching fully on; false in linear operation at low gate drive.

miller-effect.title: From f_T to capacitance
miller-effect.prompt: A transistor runs at 2 mA with $f_T$ = 300 MHz, C_μ = 3 pF and $\beta$ = 150. Find C_π and f_$\beta$.

solution.answer: $C_\pi$ ≈ 38 pF, $f_\beta$ = 2 MHz.

miller-effect.title: Two picofarads become hundreds
miller-effect.prompt: An inverting stage has gain −120 and a 4 pF capacitance from input to output. What capacitance does the input see from it?

solution.text: When the input moves by $v$, the output moves by $-120v$, so the capacitor sees $121v$.

solution.answer: 484 pF.

miller-effect.title: Predict the corner
miller-effect.prompt: A common-emitter stage runs at 0.5 mA ($\beta$ = 100) with $R_C$ = 20 kΩ, driven from 2 kΩ, with C_π = 8 pF and C_μ = 3 pF. Estimate its −3 dB frequency.
miller-effect.hint: $g_m$ $R_C$ sets the Miller multiplier; the source sees $R_s$ ∥ r_π.

solution.answer: About 94 kHz.

miller-effect.title: What the cascode buys
miller-effect.prompt: Convert the stage of the previous problem to a cascode. Estimate the new input capacitance and input pole. What new limit appears?

solution.text: Q₁ now drives the low impedance of Q₂'s emitter ($r_e$ = $1/g_m$), so its voltage gain is about −1.
The output node: 20 kΩ with about 5 pF (Q₂'s $C_\mu$ plus wiring and load).

solution.answer: $C_{in}$ ≈ 14 pF, input pole ≈ 7.9 MHz; the output pole (~1.6 MHz) now sets the bandwidth.

miller-effect.title: The Miller plateau
miller-effect.prompt: A transistor switch is driven with 0.2 mA of base current and has C_μ = 3 pF. How fast can its collector slew, and how long does a 10 V transition take at that rate?
miller-effect.hint: dV/dt ≈ $I_B$/C_μ during the active-region part of the transition.

solution.text: During the active-region transition the base voltage is nearly fixed, so the base current goes into $C_\mu$.

solution.answer: About 67 V/µs; a 10 V edge takes 0.15 µs.
